concepts/ai-heterogeneity-and-multifunct.title: AI Heterogeneity and Multifunctionality
concepts/ai-heterogeneity-and-multifunct.content:
AI Heterogeneity and Multifunctionality
Core idea
AI Heterogeneity and Multifunctionality names the reason one-size-fits-all AI regulation often fails. AI is not a single technology with one stable risk profile. Systems vary by design, data, objective, user, domain, institutional setting, and decision role.
Foundation models and generative AI deepen the problem because the same model can perform many functions. A general-purpose model can become a tutor, medical assistant, sales agent, search interface, coding assistant, bureaucratic chatbot, content recommender, or behavioral coach. The risk is therefore not only in the model; it is in the combination of model, use, user, goal, and institution.
Key distinctions

Use heterogeneity: the same system can be used for different tasks and harms.
Design heterogeneity: architectures, training data, objectives, and interfaces vary widely.
Problem heterogeneity: some domains have clear labels and low stakes, while others involve ambiguous values, scarce feedback, or severe consequences.
Multifunctionality: foundation models can support many downstream functions from the same underlying model.
Dynamic heterogeneity: systems change through updates, fine-tuning, feedback loops, and new deployment contexts.

Digital relevance
Digital nudging depends on context. The same design feature can help, manipulate, simplify, obscure, inform, exploit, or protect depending on its target, timing, objective, and user vulnerability. AI multifunctionality makes this sharper: a generative assistant can nudge by explaining, ranking, warning, framing, discouraging, drafting, or silently filtering options.
For the course, this concept explains why governance must move from static taxonomies to lifecycle management, reason-giving, audits, and institutional accountability.

concepts/adaptive-armor.title: Adaptive Armor
concepts/adaptive-armor.content:
Adaptive Armor
Core idea
Adaptive Armor is Ludwig, Mullainathan, Pink, and Rambachan’s term for algorithms that help users navigate dynamic and adversarial choice environments. The image is defensive: when firms adapt their obfuscation, shrouded attributes, or confusing designs, user-serving algorithms can adapt too.
Mechanism
Adaptive armor works by reading, comparing, translating, and reformatting complex choice environments in real time. Instead of relying only on static disclosures or one-time regulations, an algorithmic tool can surface the material information that a firm has buried or reframed.
The paper’s main example is credit-card offers. If a provider highlights rewards while hiding fees or repayment penalties, an LLM-like tool can summarize the key tradeoffs and put the dangerous terms at the top.
Digital relevance
Adaptive armor is a constructive answer to Sludge and Dark Patterns. It turns algorithmic adaptation into a user-serving capacity rather than a platform-serving one.
It is also a bridge between Smart Disclosure and Behavioral Economics 2.0. Smart disclosure gives tools machine-readable data; adaptive armor uses algorithmic interpretation to protect users when data or terms are confusing, adversarial, or strategically presented.

concepts/adversarial-choice-architecture.title: Adversarial Choice Architecture
concepts/adversarial-choice-architecture.content:
Adversarial Choice Architecture
Core idea
Adversarial Choice Architecture is the use of interface structure, information flow, friction, defaults, salience, timing, and personalization to steer users toward outcomes that primarily benefit the architect and frustrate the user’s own welfare, preferences, autonomy, or ability to refuse.
It is the broader concept behind many Dark Patterns. A dark pattern is a recognizable design pattern; adversarial choice architecture is the strategic orientation that makes the environment user-hostile.
Relation to nudging
Classical nudging is defended as Choice Architecture under a paternalistic constraint: influence should be easy to avoid and should make choosers better off by their own lights. Adversarial choice architecture keeps the behavioral machinery but removes that constraint.
This is why the issue is not simply that both nudges and dark patterns exploit automatic cognition. The difference is the governing objective:

User-serving nudges try to help people act on stable interests or reflective goals.
Adversarial choice architecture uses the same cognitive and interface levers to extract money, data, attention, consent, or continued dependence.

Mechanisms
Common mechanisms include:

asymmetric visibility between acceptance and refusal
defaults that extract data or money
hidden fees, hidden subscriptions, and drip pricing
countdowns, scarcity claims, social proof, and urgency cues
confirmshaming and emotional pressure
trick questions and confusing wording
forced registration, forced disclosure, or forced continuity
cancellation mazes, roach motel flows, and other forms of Sludge
personalization that targets vulnerability or momentary susceptibility
A/B tests that optimize conversion, retention, or engagement without measuring user welfare

Why the concept matters
Adversarial choice architecture keeps the course from reducing dark patterns to a list of examples. It names a structural problem: the platform controls the user’s choice environment, observes behavior, tests variants, and optimizes the interface according to goals that may diverge from the user’s.
The concept also clarifies why Sludge is a method rather than the definition. Sludge is friction. It becomes adversarial when the friction predictably protects the architect’s interest against the user’s ability to refuse, exit, compare, or reverse.
Evaluation questions

What objective is the interface optimizing?
Who benefits if the design succeeds?
Are acceptance, refusal, and reversal equally visible and easy?
Does the design help the user understand the decision, or exploit what users are unlikely to notice?
Does the system learn which variants work on which users?
Would users endorse the design if they understood the metric, data, and experiment behind it?

concepts/algorithmic-accountability-and-.title: Algorithmic Accountability and Fairness
concepts/algorithmic-accountability-and-.content:
Algorithmic Accountability and Fairness
Core idea
Algorithmic Accountability and Fairness asks how algorithmic systems that rank, recommend, predict, score, filter, or guide decisions can be inspected, contested, justified, and corrected. In Digital Nudging, the issue is not only automated decision-making. It also includes algorithmic decision-guidance that shapes what people see and choose.
Yeung’s Hypernudge account connects this topic to nudging by treating Big Data guidance systems as opaque, personalized choice architecture.
The COMPAS Controversy adds the first algorithmic fairness case. Machine Bias shows how a risk score can distribute errors unequally while shaping legal decisions. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores shows why apparently reasonable fairness criteria can conflict when base rates differ and prediction is imperfect.
On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness adds a calibration-centered account of fair prediction: a score or prediction should have the same evidential meaning across groups. It also warns that unfairness can enter through the decision rule, background social conditions, or side effects even when the predictive signal itself is fair.
Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy adds that accountability requires justifying the fairness ideal itself. A platform or public agency cannot make fairness accountable merely by publishing a metric; it must explain why that metric fits the domain’s goods, harms, groups, and history.
Measuring Algorithmic Fairness adds the action rule. Accountability should explain how false positives and false negatives are weighted, who bears them, and whether the system is compounding prior injustice.
Algorithmic Decision Making and the Cost of Fairness adds that accountability should also disclose the policy objective and the cost of satisfying a fairness constraint relative to that objective.
What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? adds the sociotechnical rule. Accountability should not stop at whether a model satisfies a fairness metric. It should inspect the whole algorithmic bureaucracy: what the system optimizes, how predictions become action, what humans do with scores, whether people can understand and contest decisions, and whether the institutional role of the tool is legitimate.
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions adds the efficiency frontier: accountability should also ask whether the human-only status quo is wasting welfare or liberty. Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers adds that those gains are fragile unless evaluation handles selective labels, omitted payoffs, and human use of recommendations.
Economics in the Age of Algorithms generalizes this point. Accountability for decision aids should cover not only fairness and accuracy, but the prediction policy problem they are meant to solve, the ranking they impose, the human workflow they alter, and the economic objective they make endogenous.
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Algorithms adds an effectiveness benchmark. If an algorithmic intervention looks highly cost-effective because it improves ranking and scales cheaply, accountability should move quickly to pilot design, in situ evaluation, and monitoring of human use rather than stopping at retrospective promise.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 adds a constructive accountability target: algorithmic decision aids should be evaluated by whether they help users approach Reflective Equilibrium, not merely by predictive accuracy.
The Coglianese-Lehr and Coglianese-Crum governance cluster adds the administrative-law layer. Regulating by Robot and Transparency and Algorithmic Governance argue that algorithmic governance can be legally compatible with due process, nondelegation, reason-giving, and transparency when objectives, validation, and decision roles are explained. Administrative Law in the Automated State adds that automated administration may improve expertise and accountability, but must remain empathic. Taking Training Seriously, Regulating Multifunctionality, and Leashes, Not Guardrails then shift from legal defense to governance design: heterogeneous and multifunctional AI should be governed through Management-Based AI Regulation, Human-Guided AI Training, and active human oversight rather than static guardrails alone.
Core concerns

Opacity: users and outsiders may not know how rankings, recommendations, or prompts are generated.
Structural bias: search and recommendation systems can systematically favor some actors, groups, products, or viewpoints.
Fairness: users may receive different opportunities, prices, warnings, rankings, or burdens without knowing why.
Accountability gaps: trade secrecy, technical complexity, and platform power can block scrutiny.
Due process: predictive policing, scoring, and ranking systems can affect rights or opportunities even when no explicit command is issued.
Error distribution: similar overall accuracy can hide unequal false positive and false negative burdens across groups.
Predictive parity: scores and predictions should preserve the same evidential meaning across groups.
Error-rate parity: practical burdens from false positives and false negatives should be examined across protected groups.
Fairness metric conflict: calibration, error-rate balance, and statistical parity capture different fairness ideas and can be mutually incompatible.
Normative justification: fairness metrics should be chosen with reference to a philosophical and institutional account of the relevant harm.
Policy alignment: fairness constraints should be tested against the legitimate regulatory or policy goal, including costs and omitted values.
Sociotechnical fairness: model metrics are diagnostics inside a larger decision system, not final certificates of fairness.
Human-AI complementarity: a decision aid should account for what the human knows that the algorithm does not, and what the algorithm can predict that the human cannot.
Selective labels and omitted payoffs: algorithmic systems should be evaluated against valid counterfactuals and complete enough objective functions.
Reasoned transparency: accountable systems should explain objectives, validation, and decision roles, not merely expose raw technical artifacts.
Lifecycle governance: AI systems should be governed through training, testing, deployment, auditing, monitoring, and revision.
Empathy and contestability: automated systems should preserve human responsiveness when decisions affect dignity, rights, welfare, or opportunity.

Digital relevance
Hypernudges can produce unfairness without a formal denial. A user may simply be shown different options, nudged away from opportunities, excluded from attention, or steered through a narrower choice environment. This makes fairness harder to see and harder to challenge.
For the course, algorithmic accountability should cover both hard decisions and soft steering. The COMPAS material is useful because it makes visible a pattern that also appears in digital environments: a system may only guide or recommend, yet its scores become authoritative inside an institutional workflow.
For Behavioral Economics 2.0, accountability should also cover whether tools amplify observed mistakes, substitute designer preferences, or genuinely support agency.
Narayanan’s category-error argument is especially important for digital nudging because ranking, recommendation, personalization, and experimentation are usually distributed across many technical and organizational parts. A fair digital nudge cannot be certified by one metric if the surrounding system hides objectives, blocks contestation, or steers people through unequal friction and exposure.
The administrative-law cluster adds an implementation frame for that system-level view. Digital nudging needs more than model metrics and interface disclosures; it needs reasoned transparency, lifecycle oversight, human-guided training, risk management, and escalation paths. This is especially important for AI assistants and foundation-model interfaces whose multifunctionality makes fixed feature-level rules incomplete.

concepts/algorithmic-decision-support-ef.title: Algorithmic Decision Support Efficiency
concepts/algorithmic-decision-support-ef.content:
Algorithmic Decision Support Efficiency
Core idea
Algorithmic Decision Support Efficiency is the claim that algorithmic decision aids should be evaluated by whether they improve the decision frontier, not merely by whether they predict accurately. In judicial bail, the frontier is between crime and incarceration: can a system reduce crime without increasing jail, or reduce jail without increasing crime?
The central course example is Human Decisions and Machine Predictions. Kleinberg et al. estimate that an algorithmic release rule could reduce crime by up to 24.7 percent at the same jailing rate, or reduce jailing by up to 41.9 percent with no increase in crime. Those numbers make efficiency a moral metric because both crime and incarceration are serious harms.
Key distinctions

Prediction accuracy versus decision quality: a model can predict well without improving the decision rule.
Efficiency versus cost-cutting: the relevant gains are not merely administrative; they concern avoided crime, avoided detention, and better allocation of coercive burdens.
Human-only baseline versus algorithmic aid: the benchmark is not an ideal judge but the observed pattern of human decisions.
Automation versus decision support: the same prediction can be used as an automated rule, an advisory score, or a structured prompt for human judgment.
Efficiency versus fairness: efficiency gains do not erase fairness concerns, but fairness concerns do not erase the moral importance of avoidable harm.
Local frontier versus full welfare: a crime/incarceration frontier can omit due process, dignity, racial meaning, long-term effects, and broader institutional reform.

Evidence and debate
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions supplies the empirical anchor. The authors use New York City bail data and judge leniency variation to compare existing judge decisions with algorithmic release rules. The main result is not simply that the algorithm predicts risk; it is that algorithmic ranking could improve the crime/incarceration trade-off.
Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers supplies the implementation theory. Algorithms can remedy human fallibility, but they are fragile. Efficiency only materializes when builders handle Selective Labels, Omitted Payoff Bias, and the Override Problem.
Economics in the Age of Algorithms supplies the summary frame. Mullainathan treats the bail result as one instance of a broader class: Prediction Policy Problems. Algorithmic decision aids can be unusually cost-effective because they scale cheaply, improve misranked cases, and operate against human decision systems that leave avoidable welfare and liberty losses on the table.
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Algorithms reinforces the effectiveness argument using MVPF comparisons across criminal justice, education, health, and workplace safety. The paper’s strongest teaching contribution is the mechanism: algorithmic interventions can look extraordinarily effective when they improve the ranking of cases and operate at scale with low marginal cost.
This concept therefore sits beside, not above, Fairness Metrics and Sociotechnical Fairness. Efficiency matters because human systems waste welfare and liberty. Sociotechnical critique matters because efficiency estimates can be misleading if the wrong outcome, payoff function, or institutional unit is evaluated.
Practical or policy relevance
For Digital Nudging, efficiency asks whether algorithmic assistance actually improves the user’s or institution’s decision problem. A recommender, fraud screen, triage dashboard, or AI assistant should be judged by the outcomes it changes, the burdens it shifts, and the alternatives it makes possible.
The course should teach this as a double lesson: digital systems can outperform unaided human judgment, but only when the evaluation target is the whole decision workflow.

concepts/algorithmic-fairness-as-politic.title: Algorithmic Fairness as Political Philosophy
concepts/algorithmic-fairness-as-politic.content:
Algorithmic Fairness as Political Philosophy
Core idea
Algorithmic Fairness as Political Philosophy is the view that fairness and bias in algorithmic systems cannot be defined by statistical metrics alone. A metric operationalizes a prior normative theory about discrimination, equality, justice, responsibility, harm, opportunity, representation, or legitimate differential treatment.
In the course sequence, this page marks the turn from metrics to normative theory. Fairness Metrics describe possible mathematical criteria; political philosophy helps decide which criterion, if any, fits the moral problem.
Key distinctions

Metric versus ideal: a fairness metric is a technical proxy for a normative ideal, not the ideal itself.
Discrimination versus fairness: a system may be unfair without being discriminatory in the classic sense, and a discrimination account may not cover every algorithmic harm.
Mental-state accounts: if discrimination requires animus, contempt, or disrespect, algorithmic systems raise attribution problems.
Individual treatment accounts: if discrimination is wrong because it fails to treat people as individuals, predictive systems are challenging because all prediction generalizes.
Egalitarian currencies: fairness may concern welfare, resources, capabilities, democratic status, opportunity, or recognition.
Spheres of justice: the right fairness criterion can differ across domains such as credit, voting, employment, criminal justice, search ranking, and platform moderation.
Deontic justice: whether a disparity is unfair depends partly on how it was produced historically and institutionally, not only on the disparity itself.
Representational harms: some algorithmic harms concern cultural representation, identity, language, visibility, or stereotypes rather than direct allocation of benefits and burdens.

Evidence and debate
Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy maps fair ML definitions onto political-philosophical debates. Binns argues that statistical criteria such as demographic parity, equality of opportunity, disparate mistreatment, and counterfactual fairness make different assumptions about what discrimination and fairness mean.
This complicates the post-COMPAS sequence. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores shows that some fairness metrics are mutually incompatible. On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness gives calibration and Predictive Parity a privileged role for fair prediction. Measuring Algorithmic Fairness then argues from a legal perspective that fair treatment is more directly connected to Error Rate Parity because fairness usually concerns action rather than belief. Algorithmic Decision Making and the Cost of Fairness adds that a metric’s value depends on how it aligns with regulatory or policy goals. Binns widens the frame: the choice among metrics and interventions depends on the philosophical account of justice appropriate to the domain. What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? widens it again: a philosophically justified metric may still be aimed at the wrong object if the full sociotechnical decision system is ignored.
Practical or policy relevance
For digital nudging, the key implication is that platform fairness cannot be solved by choosing a metric from a menu. A recommender system, content moderation tool, search engine, targeting model, or personalized interface may distribute different goods: attention, visibility, speech, opportunity, risk, protection, or persuasion. The moral stakes differ across those goods.
This means governance should require a normative justification for metric choice. Designers and regulators should ask: What is being distributed? Which groups are affected? Are disparities caused by legitimate differences, background injustice, historical exclusion, or harmful representation? Is the target equal outcome, equal opportunity, priority for the worse off, equal civic standing, or something else?
Policy alignment adds a second governance question: What is the decision system legitimately trying to accomplish, and does the metric improve that goal or obscure it?
Sociotechnical fairness adds a third question: Is the algorithm the right unit of moral analysis, or should the course evaluate the entire institution, interface, appeal structure, and decision workflow?

concepts/algorithmic-governance-and-the-.content:
Algorithmic Governance and the Automated State
Core idea
Algorithmic Governance and the Automated State names the legal and institutional framework for using algorithms in public administration and other high-stakes governance systems. The cluster moves in two stages.
The early Coglianese-Lehr papers defend legal compatibility. Machine-learning tools can fit within administrative law when agencies specify objectives, validate systems, provide reasons, preserve due process, and retain responsibility. The later Coglianese-Crum papers move from legal defense to governance design: because AI is heterogeneous, multifunctional, and dynamic, regulation should rely heavily on management-based systems, human oversight, and lifecycle risk management.
Development of the argument

Legal defense: Regulating by Robot argues that algorithmic adjudication and rulemaking can fit nondelegation, due process, equal protection, transparency, and reason-giving doctrines.
Transparency refinement: Transparency and Algorithmic Governance distinguishes fishbowl transparency from Reasoned Transparency and argues that black-box systems are not automatically barred if objectives, validation, and reasons can be explained.
Normative endpoint: Administrative Law in the Automated State argues that automation may advance expertise and accountability, but an automated state must remain empathic.
Governance design: Taking Training Seriously, Regulating Multifunctionality, and Leashes, Not Guardrails argue that modern AI requires management-based regulation, human-guided training, and flexible leashes rather than static guardrails.

Digital relevance
Digital nudging sits inside algorithmic governance whenever platforms, agencies, or AI systems steer attention, salience, ranking, defaults, or decision support. The governance problem is not only whether a nudge is individually transparent or welfare-promoting. It is whether the system that produces nudges has legitimate objectives, validation evidence, human oversight, reason-giving, contestability, and empathy.
For the course, this concept becomes the administrative-law companion to the fairness and hypernudging modules. It says that algorithmic choice architecture can be legally compatible and socially useful, but only when embedded in accountable institutions.

concepts/algorithmic-thought-partners.title: Algorithmic Thought Partners
concepts/algorithmic-thought-partners.content:
Algorithmic Thought Partners
Core idea
Algorithmic Thought Partners are AI or algorithmic systems that help people reason, understand, predict, compare, implement, and practice decisions. In Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0, they are the central mechanism through which digital nudging can become tool-building rather than only intervention design.
A thought partner does not simply choose for the user or push the user toward a preselected behavior. Its ideal role is to help the user approach Reflective Equilibrium.
Functions

Explanation: translate confusing forms, instructions, terms, or consequences.
Information: add forecasts, comparisons, and missing context that the user could not easily process alone.
Reflection: identify biases or psychological traps that may distort judgment.
Implementation: help carry out a chosen plan, such as filling forms or setting future defaults.
Practice: create repeated opportunities for rehearsal, feedback, and debiasing.

Contrast with recommendation systems
Traditional Recommendation Systems often predict what a user would choose or what similar users chose. Thought partners should instead help with what the user would choose under better information and considered judgment.
That distinction matters because observed behavior can encode mistakes. A recommender that predicts mistakes well may amplify them. A thought partner should help users reason through them.
Digital relevance
Examples include LLM explanations of court summonses, AI financial advisors, credit-card comparison tools, sunk-cost alerts, pretrial decision aids, AI agents that implement chosen actions, police training simulators, and teacher feedback systems.
The course should treat thought partners as one of the constructive frontiers of digital nudging: digital systems that enlarge agency rather than shrink it.

concepts/behavioral-economics-2.0.title: Behavioral Economics 2.0
concepts/behavioral-economics-2.0.content:
Behavioral Economics 2.0
Core idea
Behavioral Economics 2.0 is Ludwig, Mullainathan, Pink, and Rambachan’s programmatic name for a behavioral economics built around algorithmic tools rather than only behavioral interventions. The goal is to help people make decisions closer to Reflective Equilibrium, not merely to move behavior in a direction assumed to be good on average.
The concept is a positive-potential counterpart to Hypernudge. It treats AI and algorithms as possible instruments of agency, deliberation, debiasing, and welfare improvement.
Paradigm shift

Behavioral Economics 1.0: identifies systematic mistakes and designs nudges, defaults, simplifications, and reminders to improve behavior on average.
Precision nudging: uses machine learning to target the right nudge, user, timing, or format for a specified behavioral direction.
Behavioral Economics 2.0: asks which direction is right for this person and designs algorithms that help them get closer to that choice.

The shift is from intervention design to tool building. A nudge is done to someone; an algorithmic thought partner is something a person can use.
Personalized Nudging (Mills) is the systematic complement to this programmatic shift. Mills distinguishes delivery personalization from content or target personalization, while Behavioral Economics 2.0 pushes the target question further toward Reflective Equilibrium.
Core capacities

Explain confusing options and instructions.
Fill informational blind spots with prediction or external knowledge.
Highlight psychological traps such as sunk costs, projection bias, or gambler’s fallacy.
Help implement chosen actions.
Protect users in adversarial markets.
Train better judgment through repeated practice and feedback.

Digital relevance
Behavioral Economics 2.0 broadens Digital Nudging beyond interface steering. It includes decision aids, AI agents, explanatory systems, debiasing trainers, adaptive consumer protection tools, and human-AI deliberation environments.
The ethical promise is that digital systems might preserve agency better than classic nudges by helping people reason toward their own considered judgments. The risk is that the same systems could smuggle in external objectives, overfit to observed behavior, or become paternalistic under the language of assistance.

concepts/behavioral-economics.title: Behavioral Economics
concepts/behavioral-economics.content:
Behavioral Economics
Core idea
Behavioral Economics studies how real people make judgments and decisions when attention, information, cognitive capacity, emotion, self-control, social influence, and institutional design depart from the assumptions of the Econ model. In Nudge: The Final Edition, it supplies the reason nudges can work: Humans make predictable mistakes in predictable environments.
Key distinctions

Econ vs Human: Econs optimize under standard assumptions; Humans use shortcuts, forget, follow defaults, respond to frames, and care about social cues.
Fallibility vs irrationality: Thaler and Sunstein avoid treating people as foolish. Their claim is that people are fallible and environments can make decisions hard.
Judgment biases vs self-control problems: anchoring, availability, representativeness, loss aversion, and framing differ from hot-cold states, temptation, and Planner/Doer conflict.
Individual cognition vs social influence: people are shaped both by internal shortcuts and by what others appear to think or do.
Education vs design: boosting competence can help, but the book argues that good choice architecture remains necessary because many decisions are too complex, rare, or poorly timed for education alone.

Evidence and debate
Nudge - Part I Humans and Econs maps the book’s behavioral economics foundation. Chapter 1 covers heuristics, biases, framing, and Automatic/Reflective systems. Chapter 2 covers self-control, temptation, commitment devices, and mental accounting. Chapter 3 covers conformity, social norms, cascades, identity, and pluralistic ignorance.
EAST Framework shows the applied side of this tradition: behavioral regularities can be converted into intervention properties such as ease, salience, social relevance, and timing, but they still require contextual testing.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 reframes the field’s next step. If behavioral economics identifies mistakes, algorithmic behavioral economics asks whether tools can help people correct mistakes while respecting their heterogeneous preferences.
The debate for the course is not whether every bias always appears. It is whether a digital environment activates predictable vulnerabilities, and whether design can responsibly reduce error without becoming manipulative or paternalistic in an objectionable way.
Practical or policy relevance
Digital environments are rich behavioral environments. They can anchor users with suggested values, exploit inertia through autoplay or renewal, make social proof salient, hide costs, overwhelm attention, or help users by simplifying and timing decisions better. Behavioral economics gives the course its mechanism vocabulary.
Behavioral Economics 2.0 adds a tool-building vocabulary: algorithms can explain, predict, warn, implement, protect, and train, not only nudge.

concepts/compas-controversy.title: COMPAS Controversy
concepts/compas-controversy.content:
COMPAS Controversy
Core idea
The COMPAS Controversy is the debate over whether the COMPAS criminal justice risk score was racially biased and how such bias should be measured. Machine Bias made the case famous by showing asymmetric error burdens across racial groups. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores then clarified that the debate involved incompatible fairness criteria, not just competing empirical claims. On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness adds the argument that calibration or Predictive Parity has a privileged role because it keeps scores evidentially meaningful across groups. What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? reframes the case as a warning that even a metric-satisfying risk system can be unjust if the surrounding criminal justice decision system is unjust.
Key distinctions

Error burden: ProPublica emphasized that Black defendants were more likely to be falsely labeled high risk, while white defendants were more likely to be falsely labeled low risk.
Calibration: defenders of the score emphasized whether a given score meant the same empirical probability of recidivism across groups.
Predictive parity: in Hedden’s framing, a prediction or score should carry the same evidential meaning regardless of group membership.
Error-rate parity: in Hellman’s framing, the legal fairness concern is practical: whether false positive and false negative burdens are balanced similarly across protected groups.
Policy alignment: in Corbett-Davies et al.’s framing, fairness constraints should be evaluated by their effect on the policy objective and by whether group-specific thresholds are legally and normatively acceptable.
Sociotechnical fairness: in Narayanan’s framing, the fairness of COMPAS cannot be settled by the score alone; it depends on pretrial detention, judicial workflow, procedural opacity, community effects, and reform alternatives.
Overall accuracy: similar aggregate error rates can hide different kinds of mistakes across groups.
Proprietary opacity: even if a score is calibrated, defendants and the public may lack access to the full model, inputs, or validation evidence.
Decision support versus decision-making: COMPAS did not formally sentence defendants, but it entered institutional decisions through salience, framing, and authority.

Evidence and debate
The controversy begins with Broward County data and a public investigation of more than 7,000 defendants. It then becomes a general fairness debate because risk scores can be evaluated by multiple plausible criteria. If base rates differ and prediction is imperfect, calibration and equalized error rates cannot generally be achieved together.
For the course, the dispute should be presented as a bridge between journalism, statistics, law, political philosophy, policy design, and sociotechnical critique. The data show a harm pattern; the impossibility result shows that no single metric removes normative choice; Hedden shows why the calibration family still has special force for fair prediction; Hellman argues that legal fairness focuses on action and error burdens; Corbett-Davies et al. show that fairness constraints can have policy costs; Binns explains why deciding between fairness ideals requires political philosophy rather than statistical analysis alone; Narayanan asks whether metric-centered analysis misses the larger decision system.
Practical or policy relevance
COMPAS is a clean example of algorithmic choice architecture in a coercive institution. Scores can shape bail, sentencing, supervision, treatment eligibility, and parole while being framed as neutral evidence. That makes transparency, contestability, validation, and the distribution of errors central to governance.
Narayanan makes the digital-nudging analogy sharper: the score is only one part of an institutional interface that makes some futures salient, shifts responsibility, and can legitimate preemptive restriction. That is why COMPAS should now be taught as both a metrics case and a sociotechnical systems case.

concepts/choice-architecture.title: Choice Architecture
concepts/choice-architecture.content:
Choice Architecture
Core idea
Choice Architecture is the organization of the context in which people make decisions. It includes which options appear, how they are ordered, what is preselected, what is salient, what is hidden, what requires effort, what feedback users receive, and how consequences are translated into meaningful terms.
The key proposition from Nudge: The Final Edition is that choice architecture is unavoidable. A cafeteria, ballot, website, benefit form, app settings page, recommender system, or consent banner must be designed somehow.
Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice adds a useful distinction: a context can influence behavior accidentally, but a nudge is an intentional intervention in that context. That distinction matters for responsibility.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design adds the category of informational choice architecture: algorithmic systems shape decisions by ranking, filtering, suggesting, and personalizing what users see.
Key distinctions

Physical architecture vs choice architecture: both shape behavior through layout, constraints, affordances, and cues.
Intentional vs unintentional architecture: a system may steer users even when nobody set out to nudge them.
Accidental influence vs nudge: not every influence in an environment is a nudge; the nudge label is most ethically useful when an architect intentionally tries to alter behavior.
Welfare-oriented architecture vs exploitative architecture: the same tools can help users or serve the architect’s interests.
Defaults vs active choice: a system can choose what happens if the user does nothing, or it can require the user to decide.
Friction as help vs friction as Sludge: friction can prevent errors or support reflection, but can also obstruct exit, benefits, privacy, or cancellation.
Static vs dynamic architecture: digital systems can continuously modify the choice environment through Continuous Optimization and Experimentation.

Evidence and debate
Nudge - Introduction introduces choice architects through the cafeteria example and argues that no website or store lacks design. Nudge - Chapter 5 Choice Architecture provides the toolkit: make it easy, use Defaults carefully, expect error, give feedback, improve mappings, structure complex choices, curate, and make incentives salient. EAST Framework turns this design logic into a practitioner checklist for making interventions easy, attractive, social, and timely.
The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science makes the normative premise explicit. If choice architecture is unavoidable, the question shifts from whether to influence to how to govern influence through welfare, autonomy, dignity, self-government, Transparency and Publicity, and limits on Manipulation. Digital settings sharpen this question because design changes can be personalized, automated, tested, and optimized at scale.
Practical or policy relevance
Digital choice architecture includes onboarding, navigation, ranking, recommendation, notification timing, privacy settings, consent design, cancellation paths, form length, error messages, personalization, and algorithmic defaults. It is the broad design category of which digital nudges, dark patterns, and sludge are specific cases.
EAST is useful as a fast review layer for such systems: where is the friction, what attracts attention, which social cues are present, and when does the prompt arrive?
The ethics layer asks a second set of questions: whose objective is the architecture serving, can users understand and resist it, and can outsiders scrutinize the relevant rule or algorithm?
The hypernudge layer asks a third set: what data feeds the architecture, how often is it updated, is it personalized, and what optimization target governs the system?

concepts/chooser-welfare.title: Chooser Welfare
concepts/chooser-welfare.content:
Chooser Welfare
Core idea
Chooser Welfare is the standard that a nudge should help people by their own lights. In The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science, this is framed as making people better off as judged by themselves. The standard is meant to avoid both crude revealed preference and arrogant expert paternalism.
The concept matters because observed behavior may not equal welfare. People can click, consent, buy, scroll, or accept defaults while uninformed, rushed, confused, emotionally activated, or subject to self-control problems.
Key distinctions

Revealed behavior vs reflective endorsement: what a person does in a designed environment may differ from what they would endorse under better information and reflection.
Momentary preference vs second-order preference: a person may want something now while also wanting to be the kind of person who wants differently.
User welfare vs architect objective: the metric a system optimizes may belong to the platform, agency, or firm rather than the chooser.
Ex ante welfare vs ex post satisfaction: a nudge may shape preferences and then claim to satisfy them.
Delegation vs control: a person may autonomously prefer a good default or recommender rather than active choice in every domain.
General preferences vs situated preferences: people may endorse a goal in the abstract while reacting differently to concrete interventions, question framing, or levels of specificity.

Digital relevance
Digital systems often use behavioral traces as welfare proxies: clicks, dwell time, retention, engagement, completion, purchase, acceptance, or reduced churn. These measures are useful evidence, but they are not enough. They may capture compliance, habit, addiction, fatigue, path dependence, or lack of alternatives.
For digital nudging, a stronger welfare claim should connect system behavior to user-endorsed goals. Examples include explicit goal setting, post-choice satisfaction, long-term outcomes, reversibility, complaint and exit patterns, and whether users would endorse the design after learning how it works.
Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice adds a caution about the plasticity of preferences. Even asking users what interventions they accept can produce different answers depending on how abstractly or concretely the question is framed.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design adds a stronger platform metric problem. A system may optimize for engagement, relevance, time on platform, click-through, ad value, or retention while presenting the result as personalization or user convenience.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 gives the concept a constructive target: Reflective Equilibrium. Instead of inferring welfare from observed behavior or platform metrics, a digital tool should help users choose what they would endorse under feasible information and considered judgment.

concepts/continuous-optimization-and-exp.title: Continuous Optimization and Experimentation
concepts/continuous-optimization-and-exp.content:
Continuous Optimization and Experimentation
Core idea
Continuous Optimization and Experimentation names the digital-nudging capacity to modify choice architecture repeatedly as data arrive. It includes recursive feedback loops, live algorithm updates, A/B testing, multivariate testing, and other forms of platform experimentation.
Yeung’s Hypernudge account supplies the conceptual foundation: digital guidance systems can monitor behavior, update the user’s profile, alter the informational environment, and learn from the result.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 adds the constructive version: adaptive systems can protect users in changing markets, provide repeated practice, and improve decision support as environments and users change.
Mechanisms

Recursive feedback: user behavior becomes data for further intervention.
Real-time modification: the system changes prompts, rankings, defaults, or guidance in response to new data.
A/B testing: interface variants are tested against behavioral metrics such as clicks, retention, conversion, dwell time, or sharing.
Population-level learning: trends across many users are used to update interventions for individuals.
Repurposing: data collected for one service can become input for other predictive or behavioral systems.
Adaptive protection: tools can update in response to new obfuscation, shrouded attributes, or user needs.
Growth optimization: product teams can tune interfaces to maximize signups, purchases, retention, disclosure, or attention.
Regulatory evidence: the same experiments that optimize manipulation can reveal what a platform knew about user confusion, acceptance, or abandonment.

Ethical significance
Continuous optimization makes digital nudges less stable and less inspectable. A user, researcher, regulator, or teacher may not be able to reconstruct which version of the choice architecture a person encountered, why they encountered it, or what metric the system optimized.
It also blurs experimentation and service delivery. When product changes are behavioral experiments, the familiar questions from research ethics reappear: notice, consent, harm, vulnerability, debriefing, oversight, and accountability.
The dark-pattern cluster adds a sharper risk. Narayanan et al. connect dark patterns to growth hacking and A/B testing: behavioral principles such as scarcity or social proof become operational designs only after platforms test which variant works. Luguri and Strahilevitz add that firms’ own experiments can become evidence of manipulation, because they show which design increased unwanted or poorly understood choices.
Digital relevance
This concept anchors course discussions of A/B testing, growth experiments, emotional-contagion studies, algorithm changes, recommender tuning, engagement optimization, dark-pattern iteration, and algorithmic audits.
The design question is not only whether the final interface is ethical. It is whether the optimization process that discovered it is accountable and aligned with user welfare.
Behavioral Economics 2.0 adds a different optimization target: closer approximation to Reflective Equilibrium, not just higher conversion or behavior change.
Dark patterns show the opposite target: optimization for extraction. A/B testing can make a cancellation flow just hard enough, a consent banner just confusing enough, or a scarcity message just plausible enough to increase conversion without provoking complaints.

concepts/dark-pattern-regulation.title: Dark Pattern Regulation
concepts/dark-pattern-regulation.content:
Dark Pattern Regulation
Core idea
Dark Pattern Regulation concerns legal and policy responses to interface designs that steer, deceive, coerce, or burden users for the benefit of the service. It sits at the intersection of consumer protection, privacy law, data protection, competition policy, contract law, and platform governance.
The core regulatory difficulty is that dark patterns often preserve formal consent or formal choice. The user clicked, signed up, accepted, continued, or failed to cancel. Regulation therefore has to look beyond the final click to the architecture that produced it.
Regulatory rationales
The dark-pattern literature supports several rationales for intervention:

Deception: the interface hides, misstates, or delays material information.
Unfairness: the interface imposes burdens or extracts value in ways users cannot reasonably avoid.
Autonomy impairment: the design undermines authorship over one’s own decision.
Privacy violation: consent flows trick users into surrendering data or accepting tracking.
Market failure: observed choices no longer reliably express price, preference, or quality because the architecture itself drives behavior.
Competition harm: manipulative retention, hidden costs, and forced continuity can weaken switching and comparison.

Evidence and enforcement
Shining a Light on Dark Patterns is especially useful because it treats A/B testing as potential regulatory evidence. If a firm has tested a design and knows that it increases unwanted signups, suppresses cancellation, or exploits hidden information, that evidence can support a consumer-protection case.
What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? clarifies that regulatory measurement depends on the normative lens. A privacy regulator may focus on consent validity; a consumer-protection authority may focus on deception and unfairness; a competition authority may focus on switching costs, lock-in, and marketplace trust.
An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge adds the infrastructure piece: enforcement needs stable categories if regulators are going to compare cases, issue guidance, detect violations, and audit interfaces across sectors.
Digital nudging significance
Dark-pattern regulation is the legal mirror of Ethics of Nudging. Ethical nudge theory asks whether an intervention is welfare-promoting, transparent, autonomy-respecting, and easy to resist. Regulation asks when the failure of those conditions should trigger legal duties, prohibitions, audits, disclosures, consent rules, or design constraints.
For digital contexts, the most important point is that proprietary experimentation makes the evidence asymmetrical. Platforms often know which variants work, who they work on, and whether they produce confusion or regret. Regulators and users often do not.

concepts/dark-pattern-taxonomy.title: Dark Pattern Taxonomy
concepts/dark-pattern-taxonomy.content:
Dark Pattern Taxonomy
Core idea
Dark Pattern Taxonomy organizes recurring manipulative interface strategies so that researchers, teachers, regulators, designers, and auditors can identify them without treating every bad interface as unique.
The taxonomy problem has two parts. First, examples need names: hard to cancel, sneak into basket, confirmshaming, hidden costs, bad defaults, countdown timers. Second, those examples need structure: what higher-level strategy do they implement, and what normative harm do they create?
From early taxonomy to ontology
The Dark (Patterns) Side of UX Design organizes practitioner-identified patterns into five strategies: nagging, obstruction, sneaking, interface interference, and forced action.
Dark Patterns at Scale gives an empirical e-commerce taxonomy with seven categories: sneaking, urgency, misdirection, social proof, scarcity, obstruction, and forced action. Its 15 types include hidden costs, hidden subscription, countdown timer, confirmshaming, trick questions, hard to cancel, and forced enrollment.
What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? adds attributes that help evaluate patterns: asymmetry, restrictiveness, disparate treatment, covertness, deception, and information hiding.
An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge harmonizes academic and regulatory taxonomies into a three-level ontology:

High-level patterns: broad strategies such as obstruction, sneaking, interface interference, forced action, and social engineering.
Meso-level patterns: middle-level mechanisms or angles of attack.
Low-level patterns: situated interface executions that can be detected in concrete designs.

Why levels matter
Different levels answer different questions. A low-level label such as “countdown timer” helps identify a design. A meso-level category such as “urgency” explains the mechanism. A high-level category such as “social engineering” connects the mechanism to a broader strategy of steering through social and emotional pressure.
This matters for regulation and teaching because a list of examples can become obsolete quickly. A levelled ontology makes it easier to classify new digital interfaces, including AI assistants, recommender systems, consent banners, subscription flows, and gamified apps.
Course use
For the course, examples should be used to fix the concept, not to exhaust it. Students should learn to ask:

Is this pattern hiding information, creating friction, manipulating presentation, forcing disclosure, or applying social pressure?
Is the problem deception, autonomy impairment, welfare loss, privacy loss, competition harm, or legal noncompliance?
Is the pattern static, or is it being tested and personalized through Continuous Optimization and Experimentation?

concepts/dark-patterns.title: Dark Patterns
concepts/dark-patterns.content:
Dark Patterns
Core idea
Dark Patterns are interface designs that steer users toward outcomes they would not reasonably choose under clearer, less pressured, or less asymmetric conditions. They are closely related to Sludge and Manipulation, but the emphasis is on recurring digital design patterns that benefit the service by coercing, steering, deceiving, burdening, or confusing users.
For the vault, dark patterns are the negative counterpart of user-serving Digital Nudging. They use the tools of Choice Architecture to serve the architect against the user’s reflective interests. In that sense they are a family of Adversarial Choice Architecture.
What makes them dark
The “darkness” is not just that a pattern changes behavior. Nudges also change behavior. The key issue is the relationship between mechanism and objective:

the design modifies the user’s decision space or information flow;
the design benefits the service, seller, or platform;
the user is made less able to understand, refuse, compare, reverse, or exit;
the outcome is plausibly contrary to the user’s welfare, autonomy, privacy, or actual preference.

This is why Sludge is a method rather than the definition. Obstruction, cancellation mazes, and hard-to-refuse consent flows often work through sludge, but other dark patterns work through urgency, scarcity, social proof, hidden information, bad defaults, trick questions, emotional pressure, or forced disclosure.
Representative patterns
The dark-pattern literature supplies several overlapping taxonomies:

Gray et al. identify nagging, obstruction, sneaking, interface interference, and forced action.
Mathur et al. identify e-commerce categories including sneaking, urgency, misdirection, social proof, scarcity, obstruction, and forced action.
Gray et al. harmonize the field into high-level, meso-level, and low-level patterns, with obstruction, sneaking, interface interference, forced action, and social engineering as high-level families.

Examples include hidden costs, hidden subscriptions, sneak into basket, countdown timers, low-stock messages, fake or misleading social proof, confirmshaming, trick questions, visual interference, bad defaults, forced enrollment, forced continuity, Privacy Zuckering, and hard-to-cancel flows.
Empirical and institutional significance
Dark Patterns at Scale shows that dark patterns are empirically widespread in online shopping and can be supplied by third-party vendors. This makes them a platform and market-structure problem, not just a matter of isolated bad design.
Shining a Light on Dark Patterns shows causal force. Mild dark patterns more than doubled acceptance in their first experiment while avoiding much of the backlash associated with aggressive patterns. That result is central for the course: the most dangerous dark patterns may be subtle enough to remain unchallenged.
Relationship to hypernudging
Yeung’s Hypernudge account helps explain why dark patterns can become more powerful in data-driven systems. A static deceptive interface is already troubling. A continuously optimized and personalized dark pattern can learn which version works on which users, when to deploy it, and how to hide its mechanism inside normal platform operation.
Adaptive Armor is the constructive countermeasure: user-serving algorithms can help identify, translate, and neutralize shrouded attributes or confusing design choices.
Normative and legal stakes
What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? clarifies that dark patterns can be evaluated through several lenses: individual welfare, collective welfare, regulatory objectives, and autonomy. This is useful because dark patterns can harm users in different ways: financial loss, privacy invasion, cognitive burden, reduced competition, invalid consent, or loss of practical self-authorship.
Dark Pattern Regulation asks when those harms should trigger legal responses under consumer protection, data protection, privacy, contract, or competition law. The regulatory problem is that formal consent or formal choice may remain intact even when the interface architecture has made that choice practically distorted.
Course use
For teaching, dark patterns should be introduced with a few vivid examples but then generalized. The core lesson is not that countdown timers or cancellation mazes are bad in isolation. The core lesson is that digital choice architecture can be optimized for extraction. Money, data, and attention become the resources captured by designs that exploit automatic cognition, inattention, trust, urgency, social pressure, and fatigue.

concepts/defaults.title: Defaults
concepts/defaults.content:
Defaults
Core idea
Defaults are the options or outcomes that apply if a chooser does nothing. They are central to Choice Architecture because every system needs a rule for inaction, and many users follow the path of least resistance.
In Nudge: The Final Edition, defaults matter because they exploit or support inertia, status quo bias, limited attention, and the tendency to read a default as an implicit recommendation.
Key distinctions

Default vs active choice: a default governs inaction; active choice requires the user to choose before proceeding.
Default vs prompted choice: prompted choice asks users to consider an option while still leaving a background default.
Sticky default vs rejected default: defaults are less powerful when users clearly know their preferences and the default outcome is visibly bad.
Welfare-enhancing default vs self-serving default: defaults can help users or extract money, data, attention, or consent.
Personalized default: a default tailored to a user’s situation or history, which can improve fit but raises governance and privacy questions.

Evidence and debate
Nudge - Introduction introduces defaults through smartphone settings and opt-in/opt-out effects. Nudge - Chapter 5 Choice Architecture treats defaults as ubiquitous and unavoidable, while also warning that default selection can be self-serving. Nudge - Chapter 8 Sludge shows how defaults combine with friction to trap users. EAST Framework treats defaults as a central way to make beneficial action easy, while emphasizing that permission, preferences, and backfire risks matter.
The main debate concerns when defaults respect autonomy. A transparent, easily changed default may be liberty-preserving; a hidden default paired with a difficult opt-out may be manipulative sludge.
The Ethics of Influence - Chapter 7 Green by Default adds the ethical distinction between defaults, active choosing, influenced active choice, and personalized defaults. Active choice can be more respectful for contested or intimate choices, but it can also impose unnecessary cognitive costs. Personalized defaults may improve fit while raising data, privacy, error, and accountability concerns.
Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice treats background defaults as potentially non-transparent type 1 nudges when they alter automatic behavior without the user’s recognition. That does not make every default impermissible, but it raises responsibility, disclosure, and consent questions.
Practical or policy relevance
Digital defaults appear in privacy settings, notification permissions, account visibility, subscription renewal, recommendation feeds, cookie consent, security settings, double-sided printing, app onboarding, and retirement-plan enrollment. They are powerful because clicking through is often easier than configuring.
For digital nudging, the ethical question is whether the default is transparent, easy to change, welfare-enhancing by the user’s own lights, and accountable to someone other than the system operator.

concepts/east-framework.title: EAST Framework
concepts/east-framework.content:
EAST Framework
Core idea
The EAST Framework is a practical checklist for designing behavioral interventions: make the target behavior Easy, Attractive, Social, and Timely. It was developed by the Behavioural Insights Team as an accessible way to translate Behavioral Economics and Choice Architecture into intervention design.
In this vault, EAST is the quick-reference page for the characteristics of good behavioral interventions.
Quick reference



































CharacteristicDesign questionCommon toolsDigital examplesEasyWhat friction, confusion, or effort prevents action?Defaults, simplification, fewer steps, autofill, clearer instructions, reduced SludgeOne-click enrollment, short forms, default privacy choices that users can change, prefilled applicationsAttractiveWhat will draw attention and make the action feel worthwhile?Salience, framing, personalization, visual cues, incentives, gamification, feedbackHighlighted next action, personalized reminders, progress indicators, salient savings or risk informationSocialWhat do relevant others do, expect, or model?Descriptive norms, injunctive norms, peer comparison, network seeding, reciprocity, operational transparency”Most users like you completed this,” visible participation, referral flows, peer commitmentsTimelyWhen is the user most receptive or able to act?Just-in-time prompts, fresh-start moments, immediate rewards, delayed costs, planning prompts, implementation intentionsAppointment reminders, onboarding nudges, renewal warnings, plan-making chatbots, timed notifications
Key distinctions

EAST vs full methodology: EAST helps generate and refine intervention ideas, but it does not replace problem diagnosis, fieldwork, co-design, or evaluation.
Easy vs coercive: making the target behavior easy is not the same as removing meaningful alternatives.
Attractive vs manipulative: attention and framing should be user-serving and publicly defensible.
Social proof vs social backfire: norm messages can backfire if they reveal that undesirable behavior is common or invoke the wrong reference group.
Timely vs intrusive: a well-timed prompt helps at the moment of action; a poorly timed prompt becomes noise or pressure.

Evidence and debate
EAST: Four Simple Ways to Apply Behavioural Insights synthesizes a decade of behavioral intervention examples and updated evidence. Its strongest contribution for the course is not any single case study, but the organizing heuristic: interventions often work by reducing effort, increasing salience, using social context, and aligning with moments when people can act.
The report is careful about evidence. It notes replication issues, behavioral pitfalls, and the need to test interventions in context. That makes EAST useful as a starting framework, but not as a guarantee that a given intervention will work.
Practical or policy relevance
For digital nudging, EAST can be used as a fast design review:

Is the desired action easier than the alternatives?
Is the relevant information salient, understandable, and well framed?
Are social cues accurate, relevant, and unlikely to shame or backfire?
Does the intervention arrive when the user can actually act?
Have likely failure modes, user burdens, and unintended consequences been tested?

concepts/error-rate-parity.title: Error Rate Parity
concepts/error-rate-parity.content:
Error Rate Parity
Core idea
Error Rate Parity is the fairness idea that the practical burdens of algorithmic mistakes should not fall differently across protected groups. The simplest versions ask whether false positive rates or false negative rates are equal across groups. Hellman’s more precise version, error ratio parity, asks whether the ratio between false positives and false negatives is the same across groups.
For the course, this is the pragmatic or error-burden family of fairness criteria. It asks how a system’s mistakes translate into action, burden, risk, or protection.
Key distinctions

False positive rate parity: among people who do not have the target trait or outcome, groups should be equally likely to be mistakenly classified positive.
False negative rate parity: among people who do have the target trait or outcome, groups should be equally likely to be mistakenly classified negative.
Equalized odds: a combined requirement that both false positive and false negative rates are equal across groups.
Error ratio parity: Hellman’s preferred legal-philosophical criterion, focused on whether the balance between false positives and false negatives is the same across groups.
Error rates versus predictive parity: Predictive Parity asks whether a score or positive prediction has the same evidential meaning across groups; error-rate criteria ask who bears which kind of mistake.
Aggregate error rates versus marginal treatment: aggregate error disparities can reflect base rates and distributions of easy or hard cases, so they need interpretation rather than automatic condemnation.

Evidence and debate
Machine Bias made error-rate disparity vivid in the COMPAS case: Black defendants were more likely to be falsely labeled high risk, while white defendants were more likely to be falsely labeled low risk. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores shows why calibration and error-balance conditions cannot generally coexist when base rates differ and prediction is imperfect.
Measuring Algorithmic Fairness gives the legal argument for taking error rates seriously. Hellman argues that predictive parity concerns belief, while fairness usually concerns action. Because false positives and false negatives often have different moral costs, an algorithm can be practically unfair if it effectively applies a different error-cost balance to different protected groups.
Algorithmic Decision Making and the Cost of Fairness gives the policy-cost counterpoint. Corbett-Davies et al. analyze predictive equality, a false-positive-rate parity criterion, as a constraint on public-safety optimization. They show that satisfying it can require group-specific thresholds and can reduce the modeled policy objective.
What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? keeps error-rate parity in view but demotes it from a final fairness test to a diagnostic. Unequal error burdens can reveal serious harm, but equalized errors do not prove that a system is just, valid, procedurally fair, or legitimate.
Practical or policy relevance
Error rate parity is central whenever the consequence of a mistaken classification is serious: detention, denial, exclusion, intensified surveillance, loss of opportunity, or exposure to harm. In digital nudging, false positives can wrongly target users as vulnerable, risky, fraudulent, low-value, or persuadable; false negatives can fail to protect or support users who need help.
Hellman’s caution is important: error-rate disparity is not always proof of unfairness. It is a reason to investigate measurement error, biased inputs, base-rate histories, and compounding injustice, especially when the affected groups have been legally or socially disadvantaged.
Corbett-Davies et al.’s caution is complementary: error-rate parity can be costly relative to a policy goal, and the cost should be made explicit. The hard question is whether the cost is justified by the legal and moral importance of reducing the disparity.
Narayanan’s caution is broader: after asking who bears mistakes, the course must still ask whether the institution should use the predictive system, what alternatives exist, whether people can contest outputs, and whether the system shifts attention away from deeper reform.

concepts/ethics-of-nudging.title: Ethics of Nudging
concepts/ethics-of-nudging.content:
Ethics of Nudging
Core idea
Ethics of Nudging asks when behaviorally informed Choice Architecture is legitimate. The starting point from The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science is that influence cannot be avoided. Defaults, salience, order, simplification, warnings, reminders, and friction are always present somewhere. The ethical task is to justify and constrain the influence.
For the course, the core test is not just whether a design preserves formal choice. It is whether the design is user-serving, transparent enough, respectful of agency and dignity, accountable, and easy to resist or revise.
For a longer course synthesis, see Nudging and the Ethics of Nudging.
Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice adds an important responsibility claim: the fact that all contexts influence behavior does not excuse intentional nudging. Once an architect deliberately intervenes, the architect becomes responsible for ends, means, side effects, and practical avoidability.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design adds the digital power problem: when nudges are data-driven, personalized, continuously updated, and proprietary, ordinary safeguards such as notice, consent, public defensibility, and easy opt-out may not be enough.
Ethical values

Welfare: Does the nudge improve people’s lives, ideally by their own lights?
Autonomy: Does the nudge preserve meaningful agency, including usable information, reasonable effort, and practical exit?
Dignity: Does the nudge treat people respectfully rather than shaming, humiliating, infantilizing, exhausting, or exploiting them?
Self-government: Can affected people, publics, regulators, or institutions scrutinize and contest the design?

Working tests for the course

Legitimate end: the intervention should pursue a defensible goal, not merely the architect’s convenience or profit.
Chooser-centered welfare: the target behavior should plausibly serve the chooser’s reflective interests or values.
Transparency and publicity: the action, reason, and behavioral mechanism should be open to scrutiny where possible.
Ease of resistance: opting out, reversing, refusing, or choosing differently should be practically easy.
Anti-manipulation: the design should not bypass reflection in ways that undermine autonomy or dignity.
Proportionality: stronger or more hidden influence requires stronger justification.
Evidence and evaluation: the intervention should be tested for intended effects, unintended effects, distributional impacts, and drift.
Data and optimization: digital nudges should disclose or justify what data is used, what objective is optimized, and how the system changes over time.

Typology layer
Nudge Typology gives the ethics framework a practical diagnostic. Transparent nudges aimed at reflective choice are easiest to defend. Transparent automatic-behavior nudges still require responsibility for effects because they may be hard to avoid at first exposure. Non-transparent automatic-behavior nudges require stronger disclosure and accountability. Non-transparent reflective-choice nudges are the clearest manipulation cases and should face the strongest presumption against use.
Hypernudge adds a second diagnostic. A digital nudge should be evaluated as a system, not only as an interface moment: data collection, inference, personalization, experimentation, ranking, and feedback are all part of the ethical object.
Digital version
Digital nudging makes the ethics harder because the architecture is programmable, measurable, personalized, and often proprietary. A digital design can steer behavior without looking like a policy, rule, or explicit request. It may be optimized continuously through A/B tests, hidden ranking systems, and engagement objectives.
That makes the following questions central:

What objective is being optimized?
What user data is used to shape the choice architecture?
Can users understand and change the relevant settings?
Are refusal and exit as easy as entry and acceptance?
Are experiments and personalization accountable to anyone outside the firm?
Does the design support the user’s own goals or exploit a predictable bias?

concepts/fairness-impossibility-results.title: Fairness Impossibility Results
concepts/fairness-impossibility-results.content:
Fairness Impossibility Results
Core idea
Fairness Impossibility Results show that multiple plausible fairness conditions for algorithmic prediction cannot generally be satisfied at once. The foundational result currently in the vault is Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan’s theorem for risk scores: with unequal base rates and imperfect prediction, calibration within groups cannot be combined with balance for both the negative and positive classes.
Key distinctions

Structural impossibility is not the same as practical difficulty. The theorem says that some combinations of fairness demands are mathematically incompatible outside special cases.
The special cases are narrow: perfect prediction or equal base rates across groups.
The impossibility concerns fairness conditions for scores, not only binary decisions.
Impossibility does not imply ethical paralysis. It implies that institutions must choose and justify which fairness demand matters most in context.

Evidence and debate
Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores formalizes the result after the COMPAS debate. It helps explain why ProPublica and Northpointe-like defenses could each appeal to a plausible fairness idea while talking past each other.
On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness responds to pessimistic readings of these results by arguing that most non-calibration criteria are not necessary for fair prediction. Hedden’s coin-and-rooms example is meant to show that a fair and uniquely optimal predictor can violate error-rate and statistical-parity criteria even when base rates are equal. On this view, Predictive Parity or calibration has a special role because it preserves the evidential meaning of a score across groups.
Measuring Algorithmic Fairness argues that the impossibility result should not lead us to privilege predictive parity simply because it preserves meaning. Hellman treats predictive parity as epistemic and Error Rate Parity as pragmatic: fairness turns on action, error costs, and treatment.
Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy adds that impossibility results create philosophical work rather than merely technical work. If metrics conflict, the appropriate response is to ask which egalitarian, anti-discrimination, or representational ideal should govern the domain.
The result also sets up later normative readings. Once the metrics conflict, the next question is not only “which metric is mathematically correct?” but “which error, burden, right, or institutional goal should govern this setting, and is the unfairness in the prediction, the decision rule, or the surrounding institution?”
Practical or policy relevance
For digital nudging, impossibility results are a warning against treating fairness as a post-hoc technical patch. If recommender systems, targeting engines, predictive models, or eligibility scores optimize one fairness criterion, they may worsen another. Designers and regulators need an explicit account of the decision context, the affected parties, and the cost of different errors.
