concepts/fairness-metrics.title: Fairness Metrics
concepts/fairness-metrics.content:
Fairness Metrics
Core idea
Fairness Metrics are formal criteria for evaluating whether an algorithmic score, ranking, classifier, or decision rule treats groups fairly. The crucial course lesson is that these metrics are not interchangeable. Different metrics identify different harms, and some cannot be satisfied together.
Key distinctions

Calibration within groups: among people assigned a given risk score, the observed outcome rate should match that score in each group. The score has the same empirical meaning across groups.
Predictive Parity: for binary predictions, the positive predictive value of a positive prediction should be the same across groups. In the course sequence, this belongs to the same evidential-meaning family as calibration for risk scores.
Balance for the negative class: among people who do not experience the target outcome, the average assigned score should be the same across groups. This tracks the burden of being scored too risky when one would not have reoffended.
Balance for the positive class: among people who do experience the target outcome, the average assigned score should be the same across groups. This tracks the burden of being scored too low when one would have reoffended.
Error Rate Parity: in binary classification, fairness can require equal false positive rates, equal false negative rates, equalized odds, or Hellman’s error-ratio parity across groups.
Statistical parity: groups receive the favorable or unfavorable classification at the same rate. This is distinct from calibration and can be inappropriate when the target outcome or legitimate qualification rates differ.
Score versus threshold: a calibrated risk score and a binary high-risk classification can raise different fairness questions, especially when thresholds vary by context.

Evidence and debate
The COMPAS debate is the motivating case. Machine Bias centers unequal false high-risk and false low-risk labels. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores shows that calibration, balance for the negative class, and balance for the positive class cannot generally coexist when base rates differ and prediction is imperfect.
On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness then gives calibration and predictive parity a stronger philosophical role. Hedden argues that the non-calibration criteria are not necessary conditions for fairness because a manifestly fair and uniquely optimal predictor can violate them, even when base rates are equal. Calibration is special because a violation means the same score has different evidential import across groups.
Measuring Algorithmic Fairness pushes in the other direction from a legal point of view. Hellman argues that predictive parity is an epistemic criterion: it tells us what to believe about a scored person. Legal fairness usually concerns action, treatment, and the burdens of error. For that reason, error-rate and especially error-ratio criteria can be more relevant to fairness than predictive parity.
Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy reframes this whole debate. Binns argues that each metric imports assumptions from political philosophy: what counts as discrimination, which inequalities matter, whether opportunity or outcome is the target, whether brute luck or desert matters, and whether the relevant harm is distributive or representational.
Algorithmic Decision Making and the Cost of Fairness reframes metrics as constraints on policy optimization. A metric can reduce one disparity while worsening the decision system’s stated goal. This makes metric choice a regulatory and policy question, not just a mathematical question.
What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? then reframes metrics as diagnostics inside a sociotechnical system. A parity violation can be evidence of discrimination or institutional harm, but metric satisfaction does not show that the decision system is fair, valid, legitimate, or worth building.
Practical or policy relevance
Fairness metrics are policy instruments and diagnostics, not self-standing moral verdicts. Selecting a metric decides whose errors count, what kind of equality is prioritized, and how much accuracy or efficiency may be traded for equal treatment.
For digital nudging, the same issue appears in recommendation systems, targeting, eligibility scoring, content moderation, search ranking, and personalized prompts. A system can be fair by one metric and troubling by another. Following Binns, the course should ask which philosophical account justifies the metric before treating it as an engineering objective. Following Corbett-Davies et al., it should also ask whether the metric is aligned with the legitimate policy goal. Following Narayanan, it should ask whether the metric is even evaluating the right object: the whole choice architecture and decision workflow rather than a model alone.

concepts/fairness-as-policy-alignment.title: Fairness as Policy Alignment
concepts/fairness-as-policy-alignment.content:
Fairness as Policy Alignment
Core idea
Fairness as Policy Alignment is the view that algorithmic fairness criteria should be evaluated in relation to the regulatory or policy goal of the decision system. A statistical criterion is not self-justifying. It must be connected to the objective the system is supposed to serve, the costs of different decisions, and the legal or institutional standards governing the domain.
In the course sequence, this is the regulatory-policy complement to Algorithmic Fairness as Political Philosophy. Binns asks which philosophical ideal a metric expresses. Hellman asks which action rule distributes error burdens fairly. Corbett-Davies et al. ask how a proposed fairness constraint changes the policy objective and whether that change is justified.
Key distinctions

Score fairness versus decision fairness: a calibrated score can still be used in a policy that makes poor or unfair decisions.
Metric versus constraint: fairness criteria can be modeled as constraints on an optimization problem rather than as final goals.
Objective specification: the objective must be explicit, such as public safety net of detention costs, welfare access, equal civic standing, or platform well-being.
Uniform threshold: applying the same risk threshold to all people can express one equality ideal, but may still generate group disparities.
Group-specific threshold: satisfying some fairness metrics can require thresholds that differ by group, raising legal and normative questions.
Immediate utility versus broader welfare: short-term optimization may omit long-term costs, historical injustice, support alternatives, and distributional repair.

Evidence and debate
Algorithmic Decision Making and the Cost of Fairness formalizes pretrial release as a constrained optimization problem. The authors show that common fairness criteria such as statistical parity, conditional statistical parity, and predictive equality generally require group-specific thresholds, while a public-safety-maximizing rule uses one threshold.
This does not settle the moral question. It changes the question: if a metric imposes a cost on the policy objective, is that cost justified by the domain’s legal and moral goals? The answer may differ across criminal justice, employment, education, healthcare, search ranking, recommendation, and content moderation.
What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? adds a warning about this frame. Policy alignment is broader than metric formalism, but it can still be too narrow if the objective is taken as fixed or if the analysis ignores the surrounding bureaucracy, appeal path, human discretion, historical context, and political contestation over the goal itself.
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions and Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers make the efficiency version of the same point. A prediction only improves policy if it is connected to the right decision, the right payoff function, and a valid counterfactual evaluation. Otherwise, a system can look efficient by optimizing the wrong outcome.
Practical or policy relevance
For digital nudging, policy alignment is indispensable because platforms and public systems optimize real objectives. A fairness audit should ask what the system is optimizing, what it omits, and whether the fairness constraint advances or frustrates the justified goal.
This concept is also a warning about narrow utility definitions. In pretrial release, “public safety” and “detention cost” are not the only values at stake. In digital environments, engagement, conversion, fraud prevention, or retention are rarely the right final goals without further welfare and governance justification.

concepts/human-oversight-in-ai-governanc.title: Human Oversight in AI Governance
concepts/human-oversight-in-ai-governanc.content:
Human Oversight in AI Governance
Core idea
Human Oversight in AI Governance is the requirement that responsible people remain able to guide, inspect, contest, correct, and justify AI systems. In this cluster, oversight is not a vague human-in-the-loop slogan. It has to be placed in the lifecycle: training, deployment, monitoring, auditing, explanation, escalation, and revision.
Leashes, Not Guardrails gives the image: AI can move, adapt, and explore, but the leash only works if humans keep a firm grip on the handle.
Forms of oversight

Human-guided training: human judgment shapes development before deployment.
Auditing: humans or institutions inspect whether systems perform as intended.
Documentation and disclosure: humans can reconstruct objectives, data, tests, and decisions.
Human-AI teaming: users or officials work with systems rather than merely rubber-stamping them.
Escalation and contestation: affected people can reach a human when automated treatment is wrong, harmful, or insufficiently responsive.
Empathic administration: human care remains part of institutional legitimacy, especially in high-stakes public systems.

Digital relevance
Digital nudging often works through automation that feels frictionless precisely because human responsibility disappears from view. Oversight asks who chose the objective, who approved the experiment, who can see unequal effects, who can stop the system, and who answers to affected users.
For the course, this concept connects ethics to operations. A digital nudge is not responsibly governed just because a human approved it once. Oversight must remain active as the system learns, targets, tests, and changes.

concepts/human-guided-ai-training.title: Human-Guided AI Training
concepts/human-guided-ai-training.content:
Human-Guided AI Training
Core idea
Human-Guided AI Training is the idea that human oversight should shape how AI systems are trained and developed, not merely how they are monitored after deployment. Humans can contribute domain judgment, salience, normative constraints, examples of acceptable and unacceptable reasoning, error diagnosis, and evaluation standards.
Taking Training Seriously treats human-guided training as a natural consequence of Management-Based AI Regulation. If organizations are legally required to manage AI risks, then one of the most important risk-management points is upstream in the training pipeline.
Why training matters

Training choices shape what the model learns to optimize, ignore, explain, and reproduce.
Data-only training can encode historical artifacts, proxy variables, spurious correlations, or socially unacceptable patterns.
Human guidance can help align models with human-recognizable concepts, reasons, and errors.
Explainability can improve when systems are trained around human-salient features or feedback.
Fairness work is easier when risk signals are incorporated during development rather than patched after deployment.

Digital relevance
Digital nudging systems often learn from engagement, conversion, retention, complaint rates, and short-term behavior. Human-guided training asks whether those signals are enough. A recommender or AI assistant may optimize behavior while missing autonomy, welfare, dignity, context, or downstream harm.
For the course, this concept becomes a design principle: governance of digital choice architecture should inspect the training objective, training data, feedback signals, human review process, and evaluation criteria before the system is allowed to steer users at scale.

concepts/hypernudge.title: Hypernudge
concepts/hypernudge.content:
Hypernudge
Core idea
Hypernudge is Karen Yeung’s term for Big Data-driven digital decision-guidance systems that configure a user’s informational Choice Architecture in personalized, dynamic, continuously updated ways. A hypernudge leaves the user as the formal decision-maker, but shapes the environment of attention, salience, ranking, and recommendation in directions preferred by the choice architect.
The concept is foundational for Digital Nudging because it identifies what is new about digital nudging: not merely that nudges occur on screens, but that they can be driven by data, algorithms, personalization, and feedback loops.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 should be read as a counterpoint. The same digital capacities that make hypernudging powerful can also be redirected toward user-serving thought partnership, adaptive protection, and debiasing.
Distinguishing features

Networked: the nudge operates in connected digital environments that collect and exchange data.
Personalized: the choice environment is tailored to a user’s profile, behavior, inferred preferences, and context.
Dynamic: the intervention can change as the user and environment change.
Continuously updated: the system can refine rules and prompts through ongoing feedback.
Pervasive: the intervention can operate across everyday digital services.
Opaque: the mechanism may be hidden in models, rankings, platform experiments, or proprietary systems.
Scalable: a single system can shape the informational environment of millions of people.

Mechanism
Yeung frames hypernudging as a self-contained cybernetic system. It gathers information, sets or updates standards, modifies behavior through the choice environment, observes the response, and feeds the result back into the system.
The central mechanism is informational choice architecture. Search rankings, feeds, recommendations, navigation suggestions, and predictive prompts determine which options are visible, salient, credible, easy, or framed as relevant.
Ethical stakes
Hypernudging intensifies the usual ethics of nudging. A static default or prompt can be inspected and debated. A hypernudge may be personalized, experimental, and invisible to the user. It may also optimize for engagement, revenue, data extraction, or institutional convenience rather than Chooser Welfare.
This makes Transparency and Publicity, Privacy and Consent, Algorithmic Accountability and Fairness, and Manipulation central to the concept.
The positive-potential question is whether hypernudge-like infrastructure can be governed so that it functions as Algorithmic Thought Partners or Adaptive Armor rather than opaque behavioral control.

concepts/management-based-ai-regulation.title: Management-Based AI Regulation
concepts/management-based-ai-regulation.content:
Management-Based AI Regulation
Core idea
Management-Based AI Regulation governs AI by requiring organizations to create and maintain internal systems for identifying, assessing, mitigating, documenting, auditing, and revising risks. It is especially useful when regulators cannot sensibly prescribe every permitted design choice or output in advance.
In the Coglianese-Crum cluster, management-based regulation is the answer to AI Heterogeneity and Multifunctionality. Because AI systems are dynamic, context-sensitive, and often multifunctional, rigid “guardrails” are too blunt. A better regulatory model is a flexible “leash”: developers and deployers retain room to innovate, but humans must keep an active grip on risk management.
Key elements

Risk identification: organizations must define what harms the AI system could produce in specific contexts.
Risk assessment: organizations must evaluate likelihood, severity, distribution, and uncertainty.
Technical and managerial controls: organizations must use training, testing, documentation, monitoring, and escalation procedures to reduce risks.
Human oversight: responsible humans must remain involved across the lifecycle.
Auditing and validation: regulators, third parties, or internal reviewers need evidence that the management system is not merely pro forma.
Continuous revision: controls must update as the model, users, deployment contexts, and risks change.

Digital relevance
Digital nudging systems are hard to regulate only by interface rules because ranking, personalization, defaults, recommendation, and experimentation change continuously. Management-based regulation asks a different question: does the platform have an accountable process for deciding what behavioral objectives are legitimate, what risks are monitored, what experiments are allowed, what harms trigger intervention, and what evidence is preserved?
For the course, this concept becomes a governance bridge between Hypernudge and constructive algorithmic support. Hypernudges create opacity and continuous modification; management-based regulation supplies one institutional response.

concepts/manipulation.title: Manipulation
concepts/manipulation.content:
Manipulation
Core idea
Manipulation is influence that insufficiently engages or appeals to people’s capacities for reflective and deliberative choice. In The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science, the concern is not that influence exists, or even that it sometimes works through automatic processes. The concern is that some influence bypasses reflection in ways that fail to respect autonomy and dignity.
Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice adds a sharper distinction between manipulation of behavior and manipulation of choice. A non-transparent nudge can alter automatic behavior without manipulating reflective choice, while a non-transparent nudge that shapes the premises of reflection is the stronger manipulation case.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design adds the problem of opaque algorithmic manipulation. A system can continuously personalize rankings, feeds, recommendations, and prompts in ways that users cannot detect or reconstruct.
The dark-pattern literature gives the most concrete digital form of this problem. Dark Patterns manipulate by modifying the decision space and information flow so that users are steered toward choices that benefit the service while frustrating their own welfare, privacy, or autonomy.
Key distinctions

Influence vs manipulation: all choice architecture influences; only some influence bypasses, exploits, or undermines reflection in objectionable ways.
Transparency vs justification: transparency is a safeguard, but a transparent design can still manipulate if it predictably exploits vulnerability or inattention.
Consent vs permissibility: consent can reduce the ethical problem, but it does not automatically make manipulative treatment respectful.
Nudge vs dark pattern: a nudge should be defensible by reference to the chooser’s welfare; a dark pattern uses behavioral insight to serve the architect at the user’s expense.
Sludge vs manipulation: Sludge can manipulate when friction is strategically used to exhaust, confuse, or trap users.
Manipulation of behavior vs manipulation of choice: Nudge Typology treats non-transparent automatic-behavior nudges as manipulation of behavior and non-transparent reflective-choice nudges as manipulation of choice.
Dark patterns vs legitimate persuasion: legitimate persuasion can present reasons, benefits, or recommendations; dark patterns distort the conditions under which users can recognize, evaluate, refuse, or reverse the proposal.

Digital mechanisms
Digital manipulation can appear through hidden defaults, asymmetric friction, confirmshaming, countdown pressure, scarcity cues, confusing consent banners, deceptive hierarchy, hard-to-cancel flows, algorithmic ranking, recommender loops, personalized persuasion, and notification timing.
The digital problem is structural as well as intentional. A platform can manipulate deliberately, but it can also build optimization systems that discover manipulative interfaces because those interfaces increase conversion, retention, or engagement.
Hypernudging expands the mechanism: data collection and feedback loops allow manipulation to become adaptive. The system can learn which users respond to which cues and when.
Narayanan et al. sharpen this point by connecting dark patterns to growth hacking and A/B testing. Manipulation can be discovered experimentally rather than fully planned in advance. Luguri and Strahilevitz show why subtlety matters: mild dark patterns can strongly affect behavior while avoiding the backlash that makes users realize they were pushed.
Dark-pattern manipulation
Mathur et al. are especially useful because they break dark-pattern manipulation into attributes rather than examples alone: asymmetry, restrictiveness, disparate treatment, covertness, deception, and information hiding. These attributes explain how a design can undermine reflection without literally forcing the user’s hand.
The dark-pattern cases also preserve the course’s System 1/System 2 distinction. Many patterns exploit automatic, low-effort responses: following a default, trusting a visual hierarchy, reacting to social proof, avoiding shame, or acting before a timer expires. The ethical concern is that the design is arranged to prevent slower reflection from correcting the automatic response.
Evaluation questions

Does the design help users understand the choice, or exploit what they are unlikely to notice?
Does it create urgency, fear, social pressure, or shame disproportionate to the stakes?
Are refusal, reversal, and exit as visible and easy as acceptance?
Would users still endorse the design if they knew the objective being optimized and the data used to target them?
Does the system learn which users are more vulnerable to a particular prompt, default, or pressure tactic?
Is the platform using experiments to find the most effective way to bypass refusal, exit, or deliberation?

concepts/nudge-typology.title: Nudge Typology
concepts/nudge-typology.content:
Nudge Typology
Core idea
Nudge Typology classifies nudges by two questions: what cognitive process the intervention targets, and whether the person being nudged can recognize the intention and mechanism of influence. The typology comes from Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice and is useful because it avoids treating all nudges as either harmless or manipulative.
Dimensions

Type 1 vs type 2: Type 1 nudges influence automatic behavior without engaging reflective choice. Type 2 nudges influence the attention, framing, or premises of reflective choice.
Transparent vs non-transparent: a transparent nudge lets the target reasonably reconstruct the intention behind the intervention and the means by which behavior change is pursued. A non-transparent nudge does not.

Four types

Transparent type 2: prompting reflected choice. Examples include salient prompts, feedback, prompted choice, commitment devices, and consequence displays. These are the easiest to defend when they serve Chooser Welfare.
Transparent type 1: transparent influence of automatic behavior. Examples include visible visual illusions, alarms, or environmental cues whose purpose can be recognized. These can still be hard to avoid at first exposure.
Non-transparent type 1: manipulation of behavior. Examples include hidden changes to plate size, layout, background defaults, or other features that alter automatic behavior without recognition.
Non-transparent type 2: manipulation of choice. Examples include subtle risk framing, priming, anchoring, scarcity cues, or goal substitution that shape reflective choice without epistemic transparency.

Ethical significance
The typology adds nuance to Ethics of Nudging. Transparent type 2 nudges are close to empowerment because they support reflective choice and practical resistance. Transparent type 1 nudges require responsibility for effects because users may not be able to avoid the initial automatic response. Non-transparent type 1 nudges need stronger disclosure, consent, and accountability because responsibility for behavioral effects shifts toward the architect. Non-transparent type 2 nudges are the most ethically troubling because they manipulate choice while leaving responsibility with the chooser.
Digital relevance
Digital systems can instantiate all four types. A just-in-time warning can be transparent type 2. A visible progress cue or alert tone can be transparent type 1. A hidden default, ranking rule, or layout experiment can be non-transparent type 1. A personalized scarcity message, subtly framed consent request, or targeted social proof can be non-transparent type 2.
The typology is therefore a practical diagnostic tool for digital nudging: identify the target process, inspect transparency, ask who bears responsibility, and decide what level of consent, disclosure, audit, or prohibition is appropriate.
Hypernudge complicates the typology because digital interventions can adapt over time. A nudge may be transparent to some users, non-transparent to others, or become less transparent as personalization and algorithmic ranking grow more complex.

concepts/nudge.title: Nudge
concepts/nudge.content:
Nudge
Core idea
A Nudge is a behaviorally informed change to Choice Architecture that predictably steers behavior while preserving meaningful freedom to choose otherwise. In Nudge: The Final Edition, the core tests are that options remain available, economic incentives are not substantially changed, and avoidance is easy and cheap.
For a course-level synthesis of the concept and its ethical constraints, see Nudging and the Ethics of Nudging.
For digital nudging, the concept applies to interface details such as defaults, reminders, prompts, ordering, salience, warnings, feedback, friction, recommendation structures, and simplified forms.
Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice sharpens the definition by emphasizing intentionality: a nudge is best treated as an intentional attempt to influence behavior, rather than any contextual feature that happens to influence behavior. This matters because responsibility attaches to the architect once influence is deliberate.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design marks the digital extension of the concept. A Hypernudge is not merely a nudge delivered online; it is data-driven, personalized, dynamic, and continuously updated through feedback.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 pushes beyond nudging by asking when algorithms can become tools for thought partnership rather than interventions that move people toward a predetermined target.
Key distinctions

Nudge vs mandate: a mandate requires or forbids action; a nudge preserves the option to go another way.
Nudge vs incentive: incentives change payoffs; nudges often work by changing attention, effort, salience, framing, or default status.
Nudge vs Sludge: a nudge should help users by their own lights; sludge uses friction to block or burden welfare-enhancing action.
Nudge vs boost: a boost improves competence or capability; a nudge changes the choice environment. Thaler and Sunstein argue that the two can and should often be combined.
Transparent nudge vs Manipulation: ethical nudging should be visible, publicly defensible, and compatible with reflective choice.
Type 1 vs type 2 nudge: Nudge Typology distinguishes nudges that influence automatic behavior from nudges that shape reflective choice.
Static nudge vs Hypernudge: static nudges arrange a relatively stable choice environment; hypernudges continuously reconfigure informational choice architecture using data and algorithms.
Nudge vs algorithmic thought partner: a nudge changes the environment of choice; a thought partner helps the user understand and reason about the choice.

Evidence and debate
Nudge - Introduction gives the foundational definition and examples. Nudge - Part I Humans and Econs explains why people are responsive to nudges: heuristics, self-control problems, default effects, framing, and social influence. Nudge - Chapter 4 When Do We Need a Nudge identifies conditions under which nudges are most useful. Nudge - Chapter 5 Choice Architecture gives the main design toolkit. EAST Framework gives a practitioner shorthand for many nudges and related behavioral interventions: Easy, Attractive, Social, and Timely.
The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science gives the concept its ethical framework: nudges should be evaluated through welfare, autonomy, dignity, and self-government. The book’s “as judged by themselves” standard is captured here as Chooser Welfare.
Nudge and the Manipulation of Choice adds a second debate: formal freedom to choose otherwise may not be enough, because nudges are used precisely where people are predictably fallible. The practical question is whether users can notice, understand, and resist the nudge in context.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design adds the digital debate: when nudges are personalized, dynamic, and opaque, classical tests such as opt-out, transparency, and consent become harder to apply.
Behavioral Economics 2.0 adds the paradigm debate: perhaps digital nudging should not only ask how to make nudges more precise, but how to build tools that help users reach their own considered judgments.
The main debates concern welfare, autonomy, transparency, manipulation, and sufficiency. A nudge may be too weak for externalities or serious harms; a nudge may become manipulative if the user cannot understand or easily avoid it; and a nudge may serve the architect rather than the chooser.
Practical or policy relevance
In digital systems, nudges can improve welfare by helping users complete beneficial tasks, avoid errors, compare options, remember intentions, understand consequences, and resist harmful defaults. They can also be used for platform-serving goals such as retention, engagement, data capture, or upselling. The course should therefore ask not only “does it change behavior?” but “whose welfare does the design optimize, and how easy is it to resist?”

concepts/omitted-payoff-bias.title: Omitted Payoff Bias
concepts/omitted-payoff-bias.content:
Omitted Payoff Bias
Core idea
Omitted Payoff Bias arises when an algorithm predicts one outcome even though the real decision depends on a broader payoff function. A system may look better than human decision-making on the measured outcome while worsening values that were not measured.
In bail, the omitted-payoff problem is relatively narrow because the legal decision is closely tied to flight and public-safety risk. In sentencing, by contrast, recidivism prediction is only one input among deterrence, culpability, remorse, proportionality, and social meaning.
Why it matters
Omitted payoff bias is the efficiency branch’s version of the “wrong target” problem. A system that improves prediction is not necessarily a system that improves decisions. The outcome must match the legitimate objective, and the objective must include the values the institution is supposed to serve.
Evidence and debate
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions explicitly warns that outperforming judges on one predicted outcome does not prove that the algorithm improves welfare if judges or society care about other outcomes. The authors therefore examine other possible concerns, including violent crime and racial disparities.
Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers makes omitted payoff bias one of the reasons algorithms are fragile. Poorly specified objectives can turn a useful predictor into a misleading recommendation system.
Economics in the Age of Algorithms uses omitted payoff bias to explain why prediction policy problems still need economics. The core question is not simply what the algorithm predicts, but whether the prediction matches the decision-maker’s legitimate objective function.
Practical or policy relevance
For Digital Nudging, omitted payoff bias is everywhere. Platforms may optimize engagement, conversion, watch time, click-through, churn, fraud loss, or short-term satisfaction while omitting autonomy, privacy, learning, well-being, exposure diversity, or long-term regret.
This concept links the efficiency branch to Fairness as Policy Alignment: the decision target has to be explicit, justified, and broad enough to include the relevant harms and benefits.

concepts/override-problem.title: Override Problem
concepts/override-problem.content:
Override Problem
Core idea
The Override Problem is the design problem of deciding when a human decision-maker should follow an algorithmic recommendation and when they should override it. The point is not to maximize obedience to the algorithm. The point is to combine machine and human information so that the overall decision system improves.
Key distinctions

Longer data versus wider data: algorithms can use many administrative cases, while humans may observe contextual information absent from the dataset.
Correct override versus harmful override: a human may add genuine private signal, or may add noise, bias, or overconfidence.
Explanation versus performance: explanations matter because humans need to know when the model is likely reliable, not merely because transparency is intrinsically attractive.
Decision aid versus decision maker: many algorithmic systems operate through human uptake, resistance, or reinterpretation.

Evidence and debate
Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers names the override problem as a central human-plus-machine challenge. It argues that successful deployment requires helping people learn where they have comparative advantage over the algorithm and where the algorithm has comparative advantage over them.
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions focuses mainly on the welfare frontier, but it also treats algorithms in practice as decision aids rather than final decision-makers.
Economics in the Age of Algorithms frames the problem as comparative advantage. Algorithms can extract signal from the data frame; humans may see what is missing from the data frame and may better understand the relevant payoff function. The design question is how to make those advantages complement each other.
Practical or policy relevance
For Digital Nudging, the override problem is central to AI assistants, recommender dashboards, clinical triage, moderation queues, fraud review, and personalized decision aids. A digital nudge can support agency only if users or human reviewers know when to accept, question, contest, or revise the system’s guidance.

concepts/personalized-choice-architectur.title: Personalized Choice Architecture
concepts/personalized-choice-architectur.content:
Personalized Choice Architecture
Core idea
Personalized Choice Architecture is a digital choice environment tailored to a particular user or group through data, profiles, predictions, and inferred preferences. In Yeung’s Hypernudge account, personalization is one of the decisive features that separates digital nudging from static nudges.
Personalization can make interventions more relevant and less burdensome. It can also make influence harder to detect, compare, resist, or govern.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 adds a distinction between targeting and welfare. Personalizing which nudge works best is not the same as personalizing the decision target to the user’s considered judgment.
Personalized Nudging (Mills) makes the distinction more systematic. Personalized choice architecture can personalize the delivery mechanism, the content or target, or both.
Mechanisms

User profiling: the system infers interests, habits, risks, vulnerabilities, or likely responses.
Contextual targeting: prompts and rankings change with location, time, device, prior behavior, or surrounding conditions.
Personalized salience: some options are made more visible or credible for one user than another.
Personalized defaults: the system chooses what happens if a specific user does nothing.
Personalized friction: the system can make refusal, exit, or comparison easier for some users and harder for others.
Personalized thought partnership: the system helps the user clarify options, preferences, constraints, and psychological traps.

Delivery vs content personalization
Mills distinguishes two forms of personalization:

Delivery personalization: personalizing how the nudge is delivered, such as mechanism, timing, format, channel, or frame.
Content or target personalization: personalizing what the person is nudged toward, such as the selected default, option, date, product, behavior, or contribution rate.

This distinction is central for digital nudging because the two forms have different welfare and accountability implications. Delivery personalization can be a tactic for effectiveness. Target personalization is a claim about what is good for this user.
Ethical significance
Personalized choice architecture complicates Chooser Welfare. A platform may claim to give users what they want, but the evidence for that claim may come from behavior that the platform itself shaped. It also complicates fairness: users may face different choice sets, prices, warnings, opportunities, or barriers without knowing that others see something else.
The privacy issue is structural. Personalization depends on data collection, inference, and repurposing. Strong personalization therefore links digital nudging to Privacy and Consent and Algorithmic Accountability and Fairness.
The welfare issue is equally structural. A system can personalize for persuasion, convenience, engagement, or Reflective Equilibrium. These are not the same target.
Digital relevance
Examples include social feeds, product recommendations, search results, navigation suggestions, health prompts, ad targeting, personalized prices, app onboarding, notification timing, and privacy defaults.
Personalization is not automatically manipulative. It becomes troubling when the user cannot understand the basis of the intervention, when the target is vulnerability rather than welfare, or when the system optimizes for the architect’s interests under the language of relevance or convenience.

concepts/personalized-nudging.title: Personalized Nudging
concepts/personalized-nudging.content:
Personalized Nudging
Core idea
Personalized Nudging uses data about individual or group heterogeneity to adapt nudges. The point is to avoid one-size-fits-all interventions when people differ in circumstances, preferences, biases, constraints, or responsiveness to specific nudge mechanisms.
Mills’s key contribution in Personalized Nudging (Mills) is to distinguish two forms of personalization: content or target personalization, which he calls choice personalization, and delivery personalization.
Two dimensions

Content or target personalization: the system personalizes what the user is nudged toward. Mills calls this choice personalization. The nudge mechanism is already selected, and data are used to determine the best target, option, default, date, contribution rate, or outcome for this person.
Delivery personalization: the system personalizes how the nudge is delivered. Data are used to select the nudge mechanism, timing, format, channel, frame, or salience strategy most likely to work for this person.

The difference is crucial. Delivery personalization asks how to influence. Content or target personalization asks what direction the influence should take.
Examples

Choice/content personalization: a savings default differs by user because some people under-save and others over-save.
Choice/content personalization: a fresh-start nudge uses a personally meaningful date, such as a birthday or anniversary.
Delivery personalization: one person receives a default, another receives a social-norm message, and another receives a reminder because they respond differently to nudge types.
Combined personalization: a platform chooses both the medium of an intervention and the product, option, or behavior promoted through it.

Relationship to adjacent concepts
Precision Nudging often focuses on improving the precision of delivery: the right message, timing, or nudge type for a target behavior. Personalized nudging is broader because it also includes content or target personalization.
Behavioral Economics 2.0 goes further. It asks not merely how to personalize the nudge or target, but how an algorithmic tool can help determine what the user would choose under Reflective Equilibrium.
Hypernudge is the risk-side cousin of personalized nudging: personalization plus data, continuous feedback, and opacity can become structural behavioral control.
Governance issues
Personalized nudging raises distinctive governance questions:

What data are needed to capture relevant heterogeneity?
Does personalization require Big Data, or can simpler data suffice?
Who holds the relevant data, and can public actors access it?
Does personalization undermine universality, shared experience, equal treatment, or public scrutiny?
Are users able to know why they received a different nudge or target from others?
What privacy, stewardship, and accountability duties attach to the choice architect?

concepts/precision-nudging.title: Precision Nudging
concepts/precision-nudging.content:
Precision Nudging
Core idea
Precision Nudging uses data, machine learning, or AI to select which nudge, timing, format, or target is most likely to produce a desired behavioral outcome for a particular person or situation. It is a form of personalized nudging.
The key question in precision nudging is: which intervention will best move this person toward this target behavior?
Personalized Nudging (Mills) helps clarify what “precision” might mean. Precision can apply to delivery, such as timing or nudge type, or to content, such as the target behavior or default selected for a person.
Contrast with Behavioral Economics 2.0
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 explicitly distinguishes its project from precision nudging. Precision nudging asks which treatment best nudges someone in a given direction. Behavioral Economics 2.0 asks what direction is right for this person under Reflective Equilibrium.
That contrast is important for the course. Precision nudging expands delivery precision; Behavioral Economics 2.0 tries to expand welfare precision.
Mills’s framework keeps this contrast tidy. Precision nudging can personalize delivery or content, but it does not by itself solve the reflective-equilibrium problem of whether the selected target is actually right for the user.
Relationship to hypernudging
Precision nudging overlaps with Hypernudge because both involve data-driven personalization and adaptation. The emphasis differs. Hypernudging, in Yeung’s sense, foregrounds regulation by design and the risk of opaque control. Precision nudging foregrounds improved targeting, timing, and effectiveness.

concepts/prediction-policy-problems.title: Prediction Policy Problems
concepts/prediction-policy-problems.content:
Prediction Policy Problems
Core idea
Prediction Policy Problems are decisions that hinge on predicting an outcome rather than estimating the causal effect of an intervention. The policy question is not primarily “what does this treatment do?” but “which person, case, option, or situation is most likely to have the relevant outcome?”
In the course sequence, this concept generalizes the bail example. A judge deciding whom to release, a doctor deciding whom to test, a platform deciding what to recommend, a tax authority deciding which returns to audit, and a job seeker deciding which openings to apply to can all involve prediction policy problems.
Key distinctions

Prediction versus causation: if the decision changes the payoff conditional on a predicted outcome, prediction is central; if the decision changes the outcome itself, causal inference is central.
Ranking versus treatment effect: many prediction policy problems are ranking problems in which welfare improves when high-risk, high-benefit, or high-need cases are prioritized correctly.
Prediction accuracy versus policy value: accurate prediction matters only through the decision and payoff function it supports.
Algorithmic aid versus automation: prediction policy problems often call for decision support rather than replacement of human judgment.
Evaluation versus construction: building the predictor can be comparatively easy; evaluating whether it improves decisions can be difficult.

Evidence and debate
Economics in the Age of Algorithms presents prediction policy problems as one of the main reasons algorithms should matter to economics. Human Decisions and Machine Predictions gives the canonical empirical example in bail, while Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers explains why implementation is fragile.
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Algorithms adds the public-policy effectiveness frame. Prediction policy problems often have a ranking structure, and better ranking can create large welfare gains without expanding the underlying policy. This is why algorithmic interventions can have high apparent returns when they are aimed at misranked decisions.
The concept is inseparable from Selective Labels and Omitted Payoff Bias. A prediction policy problem can look solved if one ignores missing counterfactual outcomes or evaluates only one narrow outcome. That is why Mullainathan treats the hard work as economic and econometric, not merely computational.
Practical or policy relevance
For Digital Nudging, prediction policy problems describe many algorithmic choice architectures: recommender systems, triage tools, fraud alerts, safety prompts, benefit targeting, consumer decision aids, and AI assistants. These systems decide what to show, when to intervene, whom to prioritize, and what explanation to provide.
The digital-nudging question is therefore not just whether a prediction is accurate. It is whether the prediction-guided workflow improves welfare, preserves agency, handles omitted values, and remains contestable.

concepts/predictive-parity.title: Predictive Parity
concepts/predictive-parity.content:
Predictive Parity
Core idea
Predictive Parity is the fairness idea that a prediction should have the same evidential meaning across groups. For binary predictions, this is usually stated as equal positive predictive value: among people predicted positive, the share who are actually positive should be the same across groups. For risk scores, the closely related criterion is calibration within groups: a given score should correspond to the same outcome probability across groups.
For the course, this is the “same meaning” criterion. If two people receive the same risk score, the score should not mean one level of risk for one group and a different level of risk for another.
Key distinctions

Risk-score calibration: a score such as 0.7 should indicate the same probability of the target outcome in every relevant group.
Binary predictive parity: a positive classification should have the same positive predictive value across groups.
Negative predictive value parity: a negative classification should have the same evidential meaning across groups.
Error-rate parity: predictive parity differs from equal false positive or false negative rates. A system can satisfy one and violate the other.
Epistemic versus pragmatic criteria: Hellman treats predictive parity as a criterion for what to believe, while Error Rate Parity concerns what to do and who bears mistakes.
Fair prediction versus fair use: a prediction may preserve evidential meaning while the threshold, action, institution, or social effect built on it remains unfair.

Evidence and debate
In the COMPAS Controversy, ProPublica emphasized unequal false positive and false negative burdens, while calibration-based responses emphasized that risk scores had roughly the same meaning across racial groups. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores shows why calibration and error-balance conditions cannot generally be combined when base rates differ and prediction is imperfect.
On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness gives the calibration side a philosophical defense. Hedden argues that most statistical criteria are not necessary for fairness, while calibration within groups is special because its violation means the same score carries different evidential import depending on group membership.
Measuring Algorithmic Fairness gives the legal counterweight. Hellman agrees that predictive parity preserves meaning, but argues that this makes it primarily epistemic. Because fairness usually concerns treatment and action, she argues that error-rate and error-ratio measures are more directly relevant to legal fairness.
Practical or policy relevance
Predictive parity is especially important for decision support. Judges, loan officers, clinicians, moderators, and digital platforms need to know what a score means. If the meaning varies by group, the score becomes misleading or discriminatory even before one asks what action should follow.
For digital nudging, predictive parity is a constraint on personalization and scoring. But it is not a complete governance framework. A platform could use well-calibrated scores to target harmful nudges, allocate burdens unfairly, or intensify surveillance. Predictive parity secures the meaning of the signal, not the justice of the action rule.

concepts/privacy-and-consent.title: Privacy and Consent
concepts/privacy-and-consent.content:
Privacy and Consent
Core idea
Privacy and Consent concerns the collection, processing, repurposing, and behavioral use of personal data in digital choice architecture. In Yeung’s Hypernudge account, privacy is not only about secrecy or data control. It is also about how personal data enables continuous, personalized influence.
Notice and consent problem
Yeung argues that notice-and-consent models are inadequate for Big Data hypernudging. Users rarely read or understand privacy policies, the ecosystem is too dynamic for meaningful comprehension, privacy harms are cumulative, and Big Data value often comes from unexpected future uses that could not be specified clearly at collection.
The problem is not solved by clicking “I agree.” Consent to broad data processing does not automatically authorize deception, manipulation, or behavioral experimentation.
The dark-pattern literature makes the same point at the interface level. Consent can be formally collected through screens that hide refusal, overload the user, preselect extractive options, use confusing wording, or make privacy-protective choices harder to complete. In that setting, the legal event of consent may be present while meaningful consent is absent.
Dark patterns in consent design
Dark Patterns at Scale identifies forced enrollment and privacy-invasive design as part of the e-commerce dark-pattern landscape. An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge places Privacy Zuckering, privacy mazes, forced communication or disclosure, and related consent patterns within a broader ontology of forced action, obstruction, and interface interference.
What Makes a Dark Pattern… Dark? is useful because it separates privacy loss from other harms. A design can be troubling even if the immediate monetary cost is small, because it extracts data, weakens consent, and expands future opportunities for personalization, targeting, and behavioral experimentation.
Dark Pattern Regulation connects these design issues to data-protection regimes such as GDPR. The central question is whether consent remains valid when the interface has been optimized to make refusal hard, confusing, or socially pressured.
Digital relevance
Digital nudges often depend on data. Recommendation systems, targeted prompts, personalized defaults, adaptive friction, behavioral ads, and A/B tests all require information about users or populations.
That makes privacy a design constraint, not merely a compliance notice. The course should ask what data is collected, what inferences are drawn, how data is repurposed, whether users can understand or refuse the use, and whether the resulting choice architecture serves user welfare.
Personalized Nudging (Mills) adds a public-policy data-access problem. Some personalized nudges can use simple data, but richer personalization may require data held by private firms, raising questions about data trusts, data commons, stewardship, privacy, security, and trust.
The dark-pattern cluster adds an extraction frame. Data is not only a precondition for digital nudging; it can be the thing extracted by the nudge. Consent banners, account registration, personalization prompts, and permission requests should therefore be evaluated as choice architectures in their own right.

concepts/reasoned-transparency.title: Reasoned Transparency
concepts/reasoned-transparency.content:
Reasoned Transparency
Core idea
Reasoned Transparency is transparency about why a decision or system is justified. It differs from fishbowl transparency, which is transparency about what information, data, code, records, or activities can be inspected.
In Transparency and Algorithmic Governance, Coglianese and Lehr argue that legal transparency does not always require complete access to every internal computation. It often requires an adequate public reason: the objective being pursued, the evidence used, the design choices made, the validation performed, and the role of the system in the decision.
Fishbowl vs reasoned transparency

Fishbowl transparency: access to documents, data, code, meetings, logs, or records.
Reasoned transparency: an intelligible account of purpose, justification, design, validation, and decision role.
Fishbowl transparency can support reasoned transparency, but raw access is not always enough.
Reasoned transparency can sometimes be possible even when full model internals are technically complex or proprietary.

Digital relevance
Digital nudging needs both forms. Users may need a simple reason why a recommendation, default, warning, price, ranking, or friction appeared. Regulators may need fishbowl access to experiments, objectives, data flows, and audit trails. The public may need a reasoned explanation of why the system’s behavioral influence is legitimate.
This distinction is crucial for proprietary systems. A platform might refuse to disclose source code, but it should still be able to explain what the system optimizes, how it was tested, what risks it monitors, and how affected people can contest outcomes.

concepts/recommendation-systems.title: Recommendation Systems
concepts/recommendation-systems.content:
Recommendation Systems
Core idea
Recommendation Systems are algorithmic systems that select, rank, filter, or suggest options for users. In Digital Nudging, they are a major form of informational Choice Architecture because they shape which options become visible, salient, credible, easy, or seemingly relevant.
Yeung treats search engines, product recommendation engines, navigation systems, and feeds as examples of Big Data decision-guidance. They do not force users to choose, but they channel attention and choice through ranking and suggestion.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 distinguishes ordinary recommendation from thought partnership. Traditional recommenders predict what a user or similar users would choose; algorithmic thought partners should help the user decide what they would choose under better information and reflection.
Mechanisms

Ranking: ordering options so some are more likely to be noticed or chosen.
Filtering: hiding or demoting options before the user sees them.
Prediction: inferring what a user is likely to want, click, buy, watch, or share.
Salience: making selected items stand out as relevant, popular, urgent, nearby, or recommended.
Feedback: using the user’s response to update future recommendations.

Ethical significance
Recommendation systems often present themselves as helpful personalization, but their objectives may be mixed. A recommender may optimize for relevance, revenue, engagement, sponsored placement, retention, safety, public value, or institutional convenience. Users often cannot tell which objective is operative.
This makes recommendation systems central to Transparency and Publicity, Privacy and Consent, Algorithmic Accountability and Fairness, Manipulation, and Chooser Welfare.
The Behavioral Economics 2.0 challenge is that predicting observed choice can amplify mistakes. A recommender that accurately predicts impulsive, biased, or confused behavior may be technically successful while welfare-defeating.
Digital relevance
Examples include search results, social feeds, video recommendations, product recommendations, app-store rankings, navigation suggestions, news feeds, dating matches, job ads, credit offers, and public-service triage tools.
The course should treat recommendation systems as active choice architecture, not neutral information delivery.

concepts/reflective-equilibrium.title: Reflective Equilibrium
concepts/reflective-equilibrium.content:
Reflective Equilibrium
Core idea
Reflective Equilibrium is used in Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 as the target for algorithmic behavioral support: the decision a person would make if they exercised their most considered judgment on the information feasibly available at the time.
In this vault, reflective equilibrium is closely related to Chooser Welfare. It gives a more operational form to the idea that a nudge or tool should help people by their own lights.
Key distinctions

Reflective equilibrium vs revealed preference: actual behavior may reflect confusion, missing information, bias, friction, or pressure.
Reflective equilibrium vs omniscience: the target is not perfect foresight; it is the best decision available under feasible information at the time.
Outcome vs process: the goal is the equivalent of considered judgment, not necessarily long deliberation in every case.
User direction vs intervention direction: the standard asks what direction is right for this person, not how to move them toward a preset direction.
Target personalization vs reflective equilibrium: a nudge can personalize its target without proving that the target matches the user’s considered judgment.

Digital relevance
Reflective equilibrium offers a welfare standard for digital nudging, but it also creates a hard measurement problem. If an algorithm changes choices, the course still needs to ask whether those choices are closer to the user’s considered judgment.
Possible evidence includes decision stability under new frames, responses to additional information, explicit user endorsement after explanation, long-term satisfaction, and behavioral models of known biases. None is sufficient alone.
Mills’s content-personalization category is a useful stepping stone toward this standard. It shows where the target can vary by user, while Ludwig et al. ask how the system could know which target is right.

concepts/risk-assessment-in-criminal-jus.title: Risk Assessment in Criminal Justice
concepts/risk-assessment-in-criminal-jus.content:
Risk Assessment in Criminal Justice
Core idea
Risk Assessment in Criminal Justice refers to tools that score people by predicted likelihood of future arrest, recidivism, violence, failure to appear, or supervision failure. These tools are often presented as decision support rather than automated decisions, but they can influence bail, sentencing, parole, probation, treatment eligibility, and supervision intensity.
Key distinctions

Prediction target: general rearrest, violent rearrest, failure to appear, or criminogenic need are different targets with different stakes.
Decision point: pretrial release, sentencing, parole, and treatment allocation create different error costs.
Score use: a score can inform support services, justify release, justify detention, or intensify supervision.
Transparency: proprietary models can block adversarial testing and public justification.
Fairness: the same tool can appear accurate overall while imposing different error burdens across racial groups.

Evidence and debate
Machine Bias supplies the concrete case. COMPAS scores in Broward County entered a legal environment already marked by racial inequality, jail overcrowding, and limited transparency. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores then explains why risk-score fairness is formally contested when different groups have different base rates and prediction is imperfect. On Statistical Criteria of Algorithmic Fairness adds that fair prediction may require risk scores to preserve the same evidential meaning across groups, even if downstream legal decisions require separate moral and institutional evaluation. Measuring Algorithmic Fairness argues that criminal justice fairness is especially about action and error costs: detention, release, supervision, or services. Algorithmic Decision Making and the Cost of Fairness adds the policy optimization question: what is the cost of a fairness constraint relative to the public goal the decision rule is supposed to serve? Fairness in Machine Learning: Lessons from Political Philosophy pushes the question further: criminal justice may require different fairness ideals depending on whether the relevant concern is equal civic standing, distributive burden, historical injustice, public safety, or representation.
What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? adds the broader system question. Even if a risk score were calibrated and error-balanced, pretrial detention based on predicted future crime may still be procedurally and morally troubling. The score must be evaluated within the court workflow, the legitimacy of preemptive detention, the possibility of contesting the model, the distribution of spillover harms, and the political choice to use prediction as a substitute for deeper reform.
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions opens the efficiency branch. It argues that bail prediction can improve the crime/incarceration frontier: algorithmic release rules can potentially produce much less crime at the same jail rate, or much less jail at the same crime rate. Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers then explains why that promise is conditional on sound construction, evaluation, regulation, and human-machine integration.
Economics in the Age of Algorithms turns pretrial risk assessment into the canonical example of a broader prediction policy problem: a decision where social welfare depends on predicting risk and ranking cases well, not only on estimating a causal treatment effect.
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Algorithms adds the public-finance version of the efficiency claim. If a pretrial decision aid produces even a fraction of the potential detention reduction, the avoided jail costs can make the intervention highly cost-effective.
Practical or policy relevance
This concept connects the fairness module to digital nudging because criminal justice risk tools shape human choice environments. A score makes some facts salient, frames a person as risky or safe, and can shift responsibility from a judge or officer to an apparently objective system.
The efficiency branch asks whether predictive tools can reduce jail without increasing crime, or reduce crime without increasing jail. The fairness branch asks what such gains omit if they ignore unequal errors, social meaning, rights, or institutional context.
The sociotechnical branch asks what the tool does to the institution itself: which decisions it makes salient, which alternatives it forecloses, how it changes human discretion, and whether it turns a political problem into an apparently technical one.

concepts/selective-labels.title: Selective Labels
concepts/selective-labels.content:
Selective Labels
Core idea
Selective Labels are missing outcome labels caused by prior human decisions. In bail, we observe whether released defendants fail to appear or are rearrested, but we do not observe what detained defendants would have done if released. The label is selective because the human decision controls whether the outcome can be observed.
Why it matters
Selective labels make it hard to compare human decisions with algorithmic predictions. If an algorithm recommends releasing someone whom judges detained, the relevant outcome is counterfactual. A naive evaluation can either overstate or understate the algorithm’s value depending on how the missing labels are handled.
Evidence and debate
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions treats selective labels as a central evaluation problem. The authors use judge leniency and quasi-random assignment to construct comparisons that do not simply assume judges have no private information.
Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers generalizes the point. Selective labels appear in hiring, predictive policing, parole, and other domains where past decisions determine which outcomes enter the training or evaluation data.
Economics in the Age of Algorithms turns selective labels into a general warning for prediction policy problems: ignoring missing counterfactual labels can make algorithms look better than human decision-makers by assuming away the human’s possible private information.
Practical or policy relevance
For Digital Nudging, selective labels appear whenever a platform only observes outcomes for options it showed, users it targeted, cases it escalated, or choices it allowed. Recommender systems, fraud tools, and personalized interventions can all inherit blind spots from earlier decisions.

concepts/sludge.title: Sludge
concepts/sludge.content:
Sludge
Core idea
Sludge is friction in Choice Architecture that makes it harder for people to obtain outcomes that would make them better off by their own lights. It is the negative counterpart of the “make it easy” principle in Nudge: The Final Edition.
In digital settings, sludge often appears as confusing forms, hidden opt-outs, difficult cancellation paths, burdensome consent controls, unnecessary identity checks, long disclosures, shrouded fees, or asymmetric flows that make entry easy and exit hard.
In the dark-pattern cluster, sludge should be treated as a method, not the whole definition. Dark Patterns may use sludge, but they can also work through urgency, scarcity, social proof, trick questions, hidden costs, bad defaults, or emotional pressure. The deeper problem is not friction alone; it is friction used as Adversarial Choice Architecture.
Key distinctions

Sludge vs nudge: a nudge should help users choose well; sludge burdens beneficial action or easy exit.
Intentional vs incidental sludge: firms may design retention friction on purpose, while agencies may produce burden through program-integrity rules or legacy processes.
Protective friction vs exploitative friction: some friction prevents fraud, error, or impulsive harm; exploitative friction serves the architect at the user’s expense.
Administrative burden vs dark pattern: administrative burden can occur in public or private bureaucracy; dark patterns are manipulative interface designs, many of which work through sludge.
Sludge reduction vs deregulation: reducing unnecessary burden does not mean eliminating all eligibility, security, or deliberation safeguards.
Sludge as method vs dark pattern as strategy: sludge names friction; dark patterns name the extractive or autonomy-undermining use of interface architecture.

Evidence and debate
Nudge - Chapter 8 Sludge develops the concept through subscription cancellation, mail-in rebates, shrouded attributes, travel reimbursement rules, college admissions, TSA PreCheck, cookie consent, and tax filing. The chapter links sludge to Smart Disclosure because better data and simpler forms can reduce burden. EAST Framework reinforces the practical inverse: good interventions often begin by finding and reducing cognitive or practical friction.
The central debate is when friction is justified. Digital governance needs a cost-benefit account that includes users’ time, confusion, abandonment, and exclusion.
The Ethics of Influence: Government in the Age of Behavioral Science strengthens the normative diagnosis. Sludge is not only inefficient friction; it can undermine autonomy, dignity, and chooser welfare when it exhausts, confuses, or traps people. In some cases, sludge becomes a mechanism of Manipulation.
The dark-pattern literature makes this concrete. Gray et al. treat obstruction as one high-level strategy, including roach motel designs and price comparison prevention. Mathur et al. identify hard-to-cancel flows as obstruction in e-commerce. Gray et al. place roach motel, added steps, and privacy mazes within the ontology of obstruction. Luguri and Strahilevitz show that obstruction can materially increase acceptance or signup behavior.
Practical or policy relevance
Sludge is central to digital nudging because many digital harms are not explicit prohibitions but practical barriers. A privacy setting may exist but be buried; a subscription may be cancellable but only through a long flow; a benefit may be available but hidden behind a confusing website. Sludge analysis asks whether formal choice is meaningful in practice.
The ethics framework adds a proprietary-systems warning: the firm that controls the interface may also control the data needed to measure abandonment, confusion, and asymmetry between acceptance and refusal.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design extends this warning to adaptive systems. Sludge can be tested, personalized, and optimized, turning friction into a learned instrument of steering.
For the dark-pattern module, sludge is the clearest way to show how an interface can preserve a formal right while defeating its practical exercise. A user may be free to cancel, refuse tracking, compare prices, or decline an upsell, but only after navigating costs deliberately imposed by the architect.

concepts/smart-disclosure.title: Smart Disclosure
concepts/smart-disclosure.content:
Smart Disclosure
Core idea
Smart Disclosure is a disclosure strategy in which complex information is released in standardized, machine-readable form and users can access relevant data about their own past usage or purchases. In Nudge: The Final Edition, it is meant to make disclosure useful for software-mediated comparison rather than merely legally available.
Key distinctions

Formal disclosure vs usable disclosure: information can be disclosed yet remain practically unreadable.
Human-readable vs machine-readable: machine-readable disclosure allows decision tools to compare complex products and services.
Product data vs usage data: smart disclosure requires both standardized product attributes and user access to their own histories.
Choice engines vs static labels: choice engines use data to search, filter, compare, and recommend.
Transparency vs steering: smart disclosure can empower users, but the tools built on it need governance because rankings and recommendations can be self-serving.

Evidence and debate
Nudge - Chapter 7 Smart Disclosure develops the concept through phone plans, fuel economy, APR standardization, online terms, travel websites, Open Banking, energy-choice apps, grocery allergens, and platform usage histories. It builds on Nudge - Chapter 5 Choice Architecture by treating data infrastructure as a way to improve mappings and structure complex choices.
The key debate is whether data access and choice engines actually empower users or simply shift influence to intermediaries whose incentives may be opaque.
Hypernudge: Big Data as a Mode of Regulation by Design sharpens this debate. Choice engines and recommendation systems can act as user-serving decision aids, but they can also become hypernudges that optimize ranking, salience, and selection for the architect’s interests.
Practical or policy relevance
Smart disclosure is highly relevant to digital nudging because many digital choices are too complex for static labels. Machine-readable data can support comparison tools for banking, energy, subscriptions, insurance, health plans, app privacy, algorithmic recommendations, and platform terms.
The governance question is whether the data infrastructure empowers the user or simply supplies better inputs for personalized steering.
Algorithms as a Vehicle to Reflective Equilibrium: Behavioral Economics 2.0 adds a more active model: algorithmic tools can translate complex terms, surface shrouded attributes, and help users reason through consequences. This makes smart disclosure part of Adaptive Armor, not only data release.

concepts/sociotechnical-fairness.title: Sociotechnical Fairness
concepts/sociotechnical-fairness.content:
Sociotechnical Fairness
Core idea
Sociotechnical Fairness is the view that fairness is a property of a whole decision-making system, not a mathematical property of a predictive algorithm by itself. The relevant system includes the data, model, decision rule, threshold, interface, human discretion, organizational incentives, legal context, appeal procedures, and social consequences.
For the course, this is the endpoint of the first fairness branch. It preserves Fairness Metrics as useful diagnostics while rejecting the idea that satisfying a metric makes a digital or institutional system fair.
Key distinctions

Algorithm versus decision system: a model may score, rank, or predict, but fairness depends on how that output is used.
Metric as diagnostic versus metric as objective: parity failures can reveal possible harm, but parity satisfaction does not certify justice.
Discrimination versus justice: a system can avoid one measured disparity while remaining invalid, punitive, exploitative, demeaning, opaque, or badly governed.
Technical subsystem versus algorithmic bureaucracy: automated decision support belongs to a larger administrative process with goals, discretion, accountability, and politics.
Bias audit versus system audit: checking group disparities is only one part of evaluating validity, purpose, contestability, human oversight, and downstream consequences.
Replacement versus complementarity: fairness can depend on whether an algorithm replaces human judgment, assists it, disciplines it, or creates new forms of discretion.

Evidence and debate
What If Algorithmic Fairness Is a Category Error? supplies the central argument. Narayanan treats algorithmic fairness metrics as a narrow slice of a broader accountability problem. He uses COMPAS, hiring automation, social services, and algorithmic bureaucracies to show why model-level fairness can miss the more important design questions.
Human Decisions and Machine Predictions and Fragile Algorithms and Fallible Decision-Makers add the efficiency side of the sociotechnical point. Whether an algorithm improves decisions depends on how predictions, payoffs, counterfactuals, and human overrides are organized. Efficiency, like fairness, is a property of the full decision system.
This does not erase the earlier sequence. Predictive Parity can still matter because scores should have consistent evidential meaning. Error Rate Parity can still matter because mistakes impose practical burdens. Algorithmic Fairness as Political Philosophy can still matter because metrics encode theories of justice. Fairness as Policy Alignment can still matter because metrics interact with policy goals. Sociotechnical fairness says that all of these remain incomplete unless the full system is examined.
Practical or policy relevance
For Digital Nudging, sociotechnical fairness is crucial because influence often happens through soft steering rather than formal denial. A recommender system, feed, personalization engine, search ranking, consent flow, fraud screen, or AI assistant may shape opportunity and behavior through exposure, salience, friction, timing, explanation, and escalation.
A sociotechnical audit should ask what the system optimizes, whose welfare counts, how personalization changes over time, what users and regulators can see, whether people can contest outputs, how human reviewers interact with the model, and whether the system should exist in its current institutional role.
